title: [CNCF] CNCF Welcomes Twelve New Members as Organizations Look to Run AI Agents on Open, Sovereign Infrastructure
summary: Organizations join the cloud native community to strengthen security, visibility, and control for production AI Key Highlights CNCF welcomes 12 new Silver members, expanding its community across sovereign cloud, AI agent infrastructure, security and financial services. As organizations move AI agents into production, new members bring expertise in open infrastructure that supports data sovereignty, operational visibility, security and control. Enterprises, developers and platform teams gain access to a broader ecosystem of cloud native technologies and expertise to securely build, deploy and manage AI workloads across environments. KUBECON + CLOUDNATIVECON NORTH AMERICA, SALT LAKE CITY – November 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced the addition of twelve new Silver members, reinforcing the community’s focus on open, vendor-neutral infrastructure for running AI agents in production. This cohort, spanning sovereign cloud and hosting, AI agent infrastructure, container security, and financial services, broadens the ecosystem of organizations building and operating production AI. “Deploying AI agents at scale requires the same core guarantees the cloud native ecosystem has spent a decade building: choice, portability, and the ability to control your own infrastructure,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director, CNCF. “From sovereign cloud operators to specialized security and telemetry maintainers, this group of new silver members highlights how the community is expanding to support complex, autonomous AI workloads everywhere.” As organizations move AI agents from pilot to production, platform teams face rising demands for data control, operational visibility, and software supply chain trust. CNCF’s newest members reflect that shift, bringing domain expertise and technology built to run agentic workloads on open, portable infrastructure. New Silver Members The following organizations have recently joined CNCF as Silver Members: Centron is a German cloud provider on a mission to make the cloud as simple and accessible as possible – for everyone. Its ccloud³ platform offers managed Kubernetes, virtual machines, S3 object storage, and GPU compute, operated entirely from centron’s own ISO 27001- and C5-certified, GDPR-compliant data center in Germany. CIQ is the founding support and services partner for Rocky Linux and a leading provider of Enterprise Linux infrastructure. CIQ delivers secure, performant software infrastructure for the full range of modern workloads. Global enterprises, government agencies, research institutions and supercomputing centers trust CIQ to run their most advanced workloads in production, from mission-critical environments to the systems behind major scientific and AI breakthroughs. CIQ’s products include the Rocky Linux from CIQ (RLC Pro) family of operating systems, CIQ Stratum, an open source Kubernetes engine, Ascender Pro for IT automation, Fuzzball job-based container orchestration, Warewulf Pro cluster provisioning, and Apptainer, the container system built for high-performance computing, with Apptainer Pro coming soon. Cloudpunks GmbH is a cloud native IT consultancy from Germany, specializing in Kubernetes platform engineering, DevOps automation, and cloud infrastructure on AWS and Azure — covering both public cloud and on-premises environments. As a Kubernetes Certified Service Provider (KCSP) and certified AWS and Microsoft Azure partner with Kubestronaut-certified engineers, cloudpunks works embedded in customer teams to build and operate cloud native platforms, not just advise from the sideline. Emphere fixes vulnerabilities in container images at the source, inside the Dockerfiles teams already maintain. Based in Seattle, the company works to close the gap between CVE disclosure and a deployed fix across base OS packages, language runtimes, and open source libraries. FluidCloud Limited is a Cloud Cloning platform that uses proprietary Large Language Model to enable discovery, migration, and operations of entire cloud infrastructure in minutes. FluidCloud’s multi-cloud DevOps platform works across AWS, Azure, Oracle, Google Cloud, VMware, Nutanix, Vultr, and OVH to create a universally portable graph of the entire infrastructure, powering instant disaster recovery, resiliency, migration, and multi-cloud interoperability. ImageEngine Kube is a cloud native, self-hosted image optimization engine that deploys to your Kubernetes cluster via a signed Helm chart. Working alongside your existing CDN, it delivers device-aware resizing, AVIF/WebP/JPEG XL conversion, and intelligent compression—giving platform teams faster image delivery, full control over their data, security auditability, and predictable costs. Ilert GmbH is an incident management, on-call alerting, and status page platform with a built-in AI SRE, made and hosted in Germany. Paper Compute is an open intelligence platform for teams building AI agents. Its agent gateway handles model routing, inference policy, and zero-instrumentation telemetry with tapes, deployed in your own cloud. Radar is an open source Kubernetes interface for humans and AI agents that shows how everything in a live cluster connects, not just what’s in it. Teams use it through a UI built for people and an MCP server built for agents, so both can understand a cluster the way it actually works. Open-Xchange AG (OX) is the world’s largest independent email provider, and its portfolio includes ubiquitous open source software like Dovecot and PowerDNS, alongside OX App Suite and OX Cloud. OX’s philosophy is clear: keep the internet free, open, and competitive. OX achieves this by building innovative, secure, and open solutions that empower its community, partners, and customers to offer trusted alternatives to global hyperscalers. Varnish Software AB accelerates and secures the delivery of content, data, and software, from web and streaming traffic to the packages and container images that power software supply chains. About the Newest Silver End User Member CNCF also welcomes its newest Silver End User Member, an organization that actively uses cloud native technologies to drive digital transformation: Deutsche Kreditbank AG (DKB) is one of Germany’s leading digital banks, serving millions of customers as well as businesses and institutions in future-oriented industries across the country. CNCF Silver Members receive various benefits valued at over $300,000 USD, including training and educational subscriptions, event sponsorship discounts, access to The Linux Foundation’s legal resources, opportunities to join project working groups, and more. To learn more about becoming a Silver Member, visit: https://www.cncf.io/about/join/silver About Cloud Native Computing Foundation Cloud native computing empowers organizations to build and run scalable applications with an open source software stack in public, private, and hybrid clouds. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. CNCF brings together the industry’s top developers, end users, and vendors and runs the largest open source developer conferences in the world. Supported by nearly 800 members, including the world’s largest cloud computing and software companies, as well as over 200 innovative startups, CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. For more information, please visit www.cncf.io. Media Contact The Linux Foundation pr@cncf.io

title: [HashiCorp] From insight to action: improving infrastructure risk posture with Terraform and Concert
summary: Advances in AI are accelerating vulnerability discovery, uncovering previously unknown weaknesses and complex attack paths. Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning marked a major shift in the vulnerability landscape, demonstrating how frontier AI can identify vulnerabilities that have persisted through traditional testing and expert review. As discovery becomes faster and more sophisticated, organizations will face an even greater volume of findings to assess and prioritize. But finding more vulnerabilities is only the first step. To meaningfully reduce risk, teams need a way to determine which vulnerabilities matter most and a repeatable way to take action to address them. For many organizations, that path from detection to resolution remains fragmented. Disconnected workflows, manual handoffs, and complex infrastructure environments make it difficult to understand what is affected, whether a vulnerability can actually be exploited, and what changes are needed to resolve it. Until teams can turn those insights into action, vulnerabilities remain unresolved and organizations remain exposed. Improving infrastructure risk posture requires connecting vulnerability intelligence with the infrastructure context and governed workflows needed to act. In this blog, we’ll explore how Terraform and IBM Concert help organizations move from insight to action, connecting vulnerability intelligence, infrastructure context, and policy-driven governance as part of IBM’s infrastructure lifecycle management solution. The foundation for infrastructure context and governed action Before organizations can respond consistently to changing requirements, emerging vulnerabilities, or new operational needs, they need a trusted and repeatable way to make infrastructure changes. Without a common workflow for planning, reviewing, and applying these changes, organizations can struggle to translate decisions into safe, consistent action at scale. IBM Terraform has long served as the trusted foundation for defining, provisioning, and managing infrastructure as code throughout its lifecycle. By standardizing infrastructure changes through repeatable workflows, Terraform helps organizations establish a consistent operating model across increasingly complex hybrid cloud environments. At the core of Terraform’s value is the infrastructure context and governed execution it provides. Terraform configuration and state give teams a shared understanding of the infrastructure they manage, while capabilities like Infragraph extend that context into a shared substrate across IBM’s infrastructure portfolio. Accurate, timely context helps teams and agents understand what infrastructure exists, how resources are connected, and where changes may have downstream impact. Equally as important, Terraform provides the governed execution layer for acting on that context. Organizations can codify security, compliance, and operational requirements with policy as code, evaluate proposed changes against those requirements, and embed approvals and controls directly into their infrastructure workflows. Together, infrastructure context and policy-driven governance provide the foundation for controlled action at scale. These workflows become especially powerful when paired with vulnerability intelligence, creating a throughline from vulnerability discovery and prioritization to safe remediation. From vulnerability discovery to prioritized remediation As vulnerability discovery accelerates, teams are under increasing pressure to separate the findings that matter most from the noise and act before exposure turns into impact. The challenge is not simply finding more vulnerabilities, but understanding which ones can actually be exploited and determining what needs to be addressed first. IBM Concert Protect helps teams make that distinction, moving from discovery to evidence-based prioritization: Discover: IBM plans to bring Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning into IBM Concert Protect, extending discovery to previously unknown vulnerabilities, including weaknesses without existing signatures or CVE records. Mythos-powered findings are planned to enter Concert Protect alongside traditional scanner results, helping organizations expand what they can uncover without creating another disconnected source of findings. Validate: With capabilities such as Concert’s proof of exploitability, teams can determine which findings represent real-world exposure. Rather than relying solely on severity scores or exploitability predictions, the capability continuously correlates application, infrastructure, runtime, identity, network and business context to validate whether a vulnerability can actually be exploited within a customer’s environment. Remediate: Once teams understand what needs to be addressed, integrations with Terraform provide a governed path for making the required infrastructure changes. Teams can use established Terraform workflows to plan changes, evaluate them against policy, and execute them consistently across environments. The real value comes from connecting these stages into a unified, consistent vulnerability management workflow. This helps organizations mitigate infrastructure risk more effectively by uncovering more vulnerabilities, validating what matters, and taking action safely at scale. Learn more Together, Terraform and IBM Concert help organizations connect vulnerability discovery and prioritization with the infrastructure context and governed workflows needed to act, creating a more complete approach to improving risk posture across the infrastructure lifecycle. To learn more, join IBM and HashiCorp experts for Rethinking enterprise risk in the AI world on November 19, 2026 at 11 a.m. EST. The 45-minute webinar will explore how advances in AI, including Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, are reshaping vulnerability discovery, how proof of exploitability can help teams determine which risks matter most, and how Terraform can help translate prioritized findings into controlled infrastructure changes. title: [CNCF] OpenShell on Kubernetes: A guide for platform engineers
summary: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell, started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project, is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem: Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process: before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network: outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials: the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox, the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster. A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart. How a sandbox is created and run On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail. Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue (openshell/#1719) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator. Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018). OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission. Prepare the cluster. Install a CNI that enforces both ingress and egress NetworkPolicy. The demo replaces kindnet with Cilium. Then install the Agent Sandbox controller and CRDs, and then the OpenShell gateway Helm chart. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. Deleting removes the Sandbox, and owner references clean up its Pods, Service, Secrets, and PVC. The two namespace NetworkPolicies stay. If creation fails partway, the driver rolls back. OpenShell checks only the Pod settings it needs to stay safe. Which images run, how big a sandbox can get, which credentials it gets, and who can change OpenShell’s RBAC are left to the platform team. OpenShell vs. Agent Substrate Agent Substrate is another CNCF project that provides sandboxed execution for agents. Both projects applied, and were accepted, to the CNCF Sandbox in September, 2026 (#522 and #523). Both run each agent in its own sandbox on Kubernetes, but they are built differently. OpenShell uses the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project. Substrate has its own scheduler, controller, and sandbox runtime. Lin Sun’s CNCF post, Why sandboxing your agent is not enough, makes the case for Substrate: “Sandboxing your agents is necessary, but not sufficient.” Agent Sandbox is about running agents securely. Substrate is about running them securely and cheaply at scale, by suspending idle agents instead of giving each one a Pod. Agent Substrate is not meant to be used directly, but requires an orchestration layer like Agent Executor, Kagent, or possibly in the future OpenShell (more on that below). OpenShellAgent SubstrateOriginNVIDIAGoogleCNCF SandboxVoted in Sep 26, 2026Voted in Sep 28, 2026Main problemWhat may this agent do?How do we run thousands of mostly idle agents cheaply?Unit of workOne sandbox per agent: a Sandbox, a workload Pod, and a supervisor PodAn actor: an identity plus a snapshot. When active, it runs in its own sandbox inside a shared worker Pod. Workers are designed to hold many actors (–max-actors defaults to 1,000), but the autoscaling demo notes that each worker holds one actor todayKubernetes building blockAgent Sandbox. The gateway creates agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resources, and the Agent Sandbox controller reconciles themIts own WorkerPool CRD (ate.dev), which atecontroller turns into a Deployment of worker Pods. It does not use Agent SandboxRoutingThrough the gateway and the sandbox’s supervisorAn ate-target-actor header. The router resumes the actor if needed, and atunnel passes the request to its sandbox. Actors have no Pod IPCredentialsThe supervisor swaps a placeholder for the real key, only at endpoints the provider allowsThe egress gateway swaps an ate-secret:// placeholder header for the real credential. Actors and snapshots never hold the secretIdentitySupervisor identity tied to the namespace, Sandbox UID, Pod UID, and runtime generationA SPIFFE X.509 certificate per actor, valid for 1 hour, and mTLS between all components. OpenFGA access policies are in progressStateA /sandbox PVC that survives stop and startRAM and filesystem snapshots in object storage. Suspend and resume take under a second; the goal is 100 ms at p95AutoscalingHPA for the gateway (more than one replica needs external PostgreSQL) and node autoscalers. Sandbox has no /scale subresource, so HPA, KEDA, and VPA cannot target a sandbox. Each new agent is a gateway API callWorkerPool has a /scale subresource, so HPA can scale workers on how full they are (the demo runs on kind only), plus node autoscalers. Requests wait when the pool is fullMaturityv0.1.xPre-1.0. Three areas that will matter most to Kubernetes cluster admins:: How detailed the policy is. OpenShell checks each request at a supervisor that serves one sandbox. It can let curl read GitHub issues and block curl from creating one. Substrate checks traffic at a shared egress gateway, per actor and per destination host. There is work underway to natively support OpenFGA policies and allow external policy. What Kubernetes can see. Each OpenShell sandbox is a set of Kubernetes objects, so RBAC, Kyverno, audit logs, and kubectl work on it. Substrate keeps actors, templates, and egress policies in its own API, backed by PostgreSQL, so the Kubernetes API server is not on the request path. Admission control sees Substrate’s worker pools, but not the agents or their egress policies. Isolation. Substrate requires a gVisor or Cloud Hypervisor sandbox for every actor; a plain container is not supported. That is what makes its snapshots possible. OpenShell runs a standard container with Landlock and seccomp, and you can require a stronger RuntimeClass for untrusted agents. Scaling follows from this. With OpenShell, your application decides how many sandboxes to run, and you size each one when you create it, as the demo does with Kyverno defaults and caps. With Substrate, HPA scales the worker pools, and the number of agents is separate from the number of Pods. For now, choose based on your workload. If you have many bursty, mostly idle agents, such as one assistant per user, and cost per agent matters most, look at Substrate. If your agents hold real credentials and reach production systems, and you need per-request control and policy on Kubernetes objects, look at OpenShell. Many large enterprises will likely need a mix eventually, and in the future, you may be able to use both. OpenShell’s RFC 0012, merged Sep 10, 2026, makes isolation a pluggable isolation backend, separate from the supervisor that enforces policy. The team has proposed building a Substrate backend (NVIDIA/OpenShell#3362). OpenShell would keep the policy, credential, and audit controls, and Substrate would add gVisor isolation and suspend and resume that keeps memory. One blocker is fixed. #3366, merged Sep 21, means the shared contract no longer requires Landlock or seccomp evidence, so a gVisor backend can supply its own. Two pieces are still open: a versioned transport for a backend that runs in a separate process, and a lifecycle operation that keeps memory. As of Oct 11 the issue is open. A contributor has +1’d it and asked whether the maintainers would accept it, but no maintainer has replied yet. If it is accepted, you would get OpenShell’s per-request policy with Substrate’s density. Until then, the difference for admins is where policy runs. With OpenShell, Kyverno checks the sandboxes themselves. With Substrate, Kyverno checks the worker pools, and per-agent policy is set in Substrate’s own API. What Kyverno adds Kubernetes settings decide the sandbox Pod’s image, privileges, resources, credentials, and network rules. OpenShell checks some of these itself (step 6 above). RBAC and Kyverno, or other Kubernetes policy engines, help cover the rest. Start with RBAC. If only the gateway’s ServiceAccount and the Agent Sandbox controller can create Sandbox resources, other users cannot go around the gateway. Cluster-admins still can. RBAC decides who can use which verb on which resource type. It does not look at what a request contains, and it cannot add defaults. So these questions remain: Which images may agents run? How large can a sandbox get? Can an agent receive a raw API key? Can someone add wildcard permissions to an OpenShell Role, or open up the workload NetworkPolicy? Kyverno checks these at admission, for every user and ServiceAccount that sends requests to the sandbox namespace, including cluster-admins and the gateway. The demo’s kyverno-demo.sh runs six checks that RBAC cannot do. Then it creates a sandbox through OpenShell that passes all of them: ControlAttemptKyverno policyResultPod securityA Sandbox with a privileged: true containerenforce-sandbox-pod-securityDenied: “Every sandbox container must run as non-root, drop all capabilities, and disable privilege escalation.”RBACA Role named openshell-* that grants * verbs on * resourcesrestrict-openshell-rbacDenied: “OpenShell RBAC rules may not contain wildcards.”NetworkA patch that lets the openshell-sandbox-workloads NetworkPolicy allow all egressverify-openshell-network-boundaryDenied: “…may not allow direct workload egress.”Supply chainA Sandbox that uses the tag nicolaka/netshoot:v0.13enforce-sandbox-image-hygieneDenied: “Sandbox images must use immutable sha256 digest references.”ResourcesA Sandbox with no resources set, then one that asks for 8 CPU and 16Gi of memorydefault-sandbox-resources, enforce-sandbox-resource-boundsThe first gets defaults (100m CPU request). The second is denied: “at most 4 CPU, 8Gi memory, and 20Gi ephemeral storage”CredentialsA Sandbox that loads a Kubernetes Secret with envFromprotect-sandbox-credentialsDenied: “Use OpenShell providers instead of injecting Kubernetes Secrets…” A sandbox created through OpenShell with a digest-pinned image is admitted and keeps the 100m CPU request that Kyverno added. All seven policies run in Enforce mode. Six are ValidatingPolicy resources and one is a MutatingPolicy, all written in CEL. They match Sandbox resources, Roles and ClusterRoles named openshell-*, and the openshell-sandbox-workloads NetworkPolicy. The policies check the request, not the sender, so they also apply to the gateway. Even a compromised gateway cannot push a privileged, unpinned, or oversized Sandbox through admission. However, the gateway’s ServiceAccount can still create Pods and NetworkPolicies directly in the sandbox namespace. For production, extend the policies to Pods and to any NetworkPolicy that selects OpenShell workloads. The demo leaves out four more kinds of policy, because each needs signing keys or other setup first: Image verification: require Cosign signatures, SBOM and provenance attestations, and vulnerability checks for the gateway, supervisor, runtime, and agent images. Runtime class: require a RuntimeClass such as gVisor or Kata for untrusted agents. Workspace budgets: cap the number of sandboxes, their lifetime, and GPUs per workspace. Cleanup: delete idle sandboxes with Kyverno cleanup policies, and skip any under legal hold. Admission control only sees agents that OpenShell creates. A team’s own Deployment that calls api.openai.com never goes through the gateway or a supervisor. For that case, Nirmata’s Runtime for Kyverno, or other kernel monitors, run as a DaemonSet and attach eBPF programs to the Pods that a RuntimePolicy selects. It watches exec, file open, network, and DNS activity. In monitor mode it reports AI tools that nobody approved: agent CLIs such as claude or ollama, stdio MCP servers, *.gguf model files, and DNS lookups for model-provider hostnames. It writes findings as OpenReports in the Pod’s namespace. Future integrations can bring Kyverno policies to the OpenShell Supervisor for fine-grained control of sandbox operation allow and deny decisions. Closing thoughts Agents, and applications with LLM integrations, are becoming prominent workloads on Kubernetes. Admins will be asked to run them like everything else: isolated, audited, and under policy. OpenShell builds on Agent Sandbox instead of going around it, and it adds per-binary, per-request controls that Kubernetes objects cannot express. OpenShell checks the Pod settings it depends on and leaves the rest to you. This separation-of-concerns plays nicely with the CNCF ecosystem. The rest are Kubernetes objects, and admission control handles those well. Use RBAC to control who can create sandboxes. Use Kyverno to control what those sandboxes may contain, and other Kubernetes configurations, starting with the seven policies in the demo. OpenShell controls the agent, and Kyverno controls the rest. To try it yourself: git clone https://github.com/nirmata/demo-openshell cd demo-openshell ./scripts/setup.sh && ./scripts/install-cli.sh && ./scripts/verify.sh ./scripts/demo.sh # OpenShell L7 policy ./scripts/kyverno-demo.sh # Kyverno admission policies ./scripts/cleanup.sh You need Docker, kind, kubectl, Helm, curl, SSH, and nc. Then try the policies on your own OpenShell cluster and tell us what breaks. title: [HashiCorp] Secure AI credentials from discovery to remediation with Vault Radar and Vault
summary: AI development may be changing how applications are built, but many of the security problems underneath them are familiar. Applications need credentials to connect to models, cloud services, databases, development tools, and other systems. As teams experiment with new AI services and move applications toward production, those credentials can spread across repositories and development workflows just as other secrets do. An API key gets added to a configuration file to get a prototype running. A developer uses it during testing. The application evolves, the team moves on, but the credential remains. Now the organization has two problems: How do you find credentials that have ended up where they shouldn't be, and once you find them, how do you keep them from ending up there again? That is where secret discovery and secrets management need to come together. AI adds another dimension to secrets sprawl The problem starts well before a credential is compromised. A credential that lives outside an organization's secrets management practices can be difficult to inventory, monitor, and remediate. And simply searching today's code isn't necessarily enough. Credentials can persist in Git history even after they have been removed from the latest version of a file. AI applications often depend on model providers, cloud infrastructure, vector databases, and developer tooling, all of which introduce additional credentials that need to be managed securely. HCP Vault Radar is designed to identify unmanaged secrets throughout development workflows. It scans connected data sources when they're added and as new commits and pull requests are created. Deep scanning can identify secrets in Git history, and supported secret types can include an activeness check to help teams understand which findings demand attention. That applies directly to AI development. Vault Radar currently recognizes multiple OpenAI credentials as built-in secret types, including admin, project, service account, user, and API keys. All five documented OpenAI secret types support activeness checks. The broader default detection library also covers credentials for services such as AWS and Microsoft Azure, which can be part of the infrastructure surrounding an AI application. So imagine that a development team accidentally commits an OpenAI API key to a repository. Discovering it is important but it isn't the end of the story. You found an exposed credential. Now what? Finding a secret tells you where there is a problem but doesn't automatically establish where that credential should live going forward. A team can remove a credential from code, but without changing how the application receives and manages credentials, it's easy to recreate the same problem later. And source code may not be the only place that credential has surfaced. Collaboration platforms such as Confluence, Jira, Slack, and Microsoft Teams sit alongside development workflows, capturing conversations, troubleshooting, and handoffs throughout the build, test, and release lifecycle. Developers may share a credential to solve an immediate problem, only for it to remain in a message, ticket, or project page long after that work is complete. Vault Radar can scan these collaboration environments to help teams identify secrets that may otherwise remain outside traditional code-scanning efforts. Remediation should therefore address more than the individual finding. It should move the credential toward a more consistent management model. HCP Vault Dedicated provides a hosted Vault Enterprise environment for securing, storing, and controlling access to sensitive credentials including tokens, passwords, certificates, and encryption keys. The goal is a simple shift: Instead of applications and developers becoming the places where credentials are managed, Vault becomes the system responsible for managing them. For our hypothetical exposed AI key, the team can first address the compromised credential with the provider and then store the replacement credential in Vault rather than putting it back into source code. From there, the application or AI agent can be updated to retrieve the credential from Vault when it needs it, rather than relying on a secret embedded in corde or configuration. This creates a more durable response to secret exposure. The team hasn't only cleaned up one finding. It has changed how that credential is managed. Keep credentials managed without disrupting application workflows Centralizing a credential raises another practical question: How does an application get the secret it needs? Ideally, applications retrieve secrets through Vault. But that isn't practical for every environment. Vault secrets sync supports environments where secrets need to be available through other secrets managers. Secrets sync keeps Vault as the system of record while synchronizing supported secrets to destinations including AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud Secret Manager, GitHub Repository Actions, and Vercel Projects. That means remediation does not have to end with removing a key from GitHub. A team can replace the exposed credential, bring the new value under management in Vault for centralized visibility and management, and make a supported Vault-managed secret available to applications through the appropriate destination. The application can still get the credential where it needs it without putting the credential back into source code. Instead, the application code can reference the path or variable that points to where the secret is securely stored in Vault, allowing the application to retrieve it when needed rather than embedding the credential itself. Where supported, organizations can also reduce reliance on long-lived credentials by adopting short-lived or dynamically generated credentials through Vault. Turn discovery into a repeatable security practice AI may increase the number and variety of credentials organizations need to manage, but it does not require an entirely new approach to secrets security. The better approach is to connect discovery with management and to find credentials that are exposed, address the immediate exposure, and bring the replacement credential under centralized management with secure, just in time access so the same problem is less likely to happen again. With Vault Radar and Vault, organizations can turn secret discovery from a point-in-time cleanup exercise into part of an ongoing approach to managing credentials as AI development grows. title: [Kubernetes] The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
summary:
In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup. For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators, returns an error during kubeadm init, kubeadm join, and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details. The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2. Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces: cgroup v1 documentation cgroup v2 documentation Let's enumerate some known issues. active_file memory is not considered available memoryThe kubelet treats active_file memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue (kubernetes/kubernetes#43916); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value. Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection: Memory QoS is available only on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: memory.high provides throttling, while memory.min and memory.low provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model. Enabling the MemoryQoS feature gate applies memory.high throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and memoryThrottlingFactor (default 0.9). memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write memory.min or memory.low. memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to memory.min (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to memory.low (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection. The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total memory.min and memory.low reservations on a node. Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, memory.high reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel. For example, to opt in to tiered protection: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration featureGates: MemoryQoS: true memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9 The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration and account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the TieredReservation feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls. Container-aware OOM handlingOn cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults singleProcessOOMKill to false. It therefore sets memory.oom.group for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the KubeletConfiguration reference for this setting. This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, cgroup.kill is a separate administrative interface: writing 1 to it sends SIGKILL to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides memory.events counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe. Rootless supportIn cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous. Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users. This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it. What else? eBPF stories: In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files. The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF. Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is /run/cilium/cgroupv2. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default (KubeletPSI is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, CONFIG_PSI=y, and a kernel not booted with psi=0. The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and /metrics/cadvisor. When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and automaxprocs versions. CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimescgroup v1 uses cpu.shares, whereas cgroup v2 uses cpu.weight. Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact cpu.weight values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations. In-place resource updatesIn-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then  (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2. Adopting cgroup version 2RequirementsHere's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support. You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS) The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example: containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery CRI-O v1.20 or later The kubelet and the container runtime must both be configured to use the correct cgroup driver. See Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix. kernel updates around cgroup v2When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016. In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 io, memory, and pids controllers were supported. Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 cpu controller. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) support began with Linux 4.20. The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support. Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level cpu.stat file was added in Linux 5.8. The memory.high livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later. memory.peak was added in Linux 5.19. cgroup driver configurationConfigure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. If you use kubeadm to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the systemd cgroup driver, because kubeadm manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster. If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver. Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration cgroupDriver: systemd Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033, graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured cgroupDriver value. Tools and commands for troubleshootingTools and commands that you should know about cgroups: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/: Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns cgroup2fs. systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or --type=scope: List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory. bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/*: List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP. systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/*: Recursively show control group contents. systemd-cgtop: Show top control groups by their resource usage. tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice: Show Pods' related cgroups directories. How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file?Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync): kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}{"
"}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .spec.containers}{.name}{" spec	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses}{.name}{" status	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need jq). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use crictl ps -a if the container is not running: CONTAINER_ID=$(crictl ps \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.namespace=<namespace> \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.name=<pod-name> \ --name <container-name> -q | head -n1) # OCI view (not the CRI protobuf field names) crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources' # Kernel cgroup path for this container PID=$(crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq -r '.info.pid') CGROUP="/sys/fs/cgroup$(awk -F: '$1=="0"{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)" cat "$CGROUP/cpu.weight" # request.cpu → shares → weight; not a limit cat "$CGROUP/cpu.max" # limit.cpu as "quota period"; unlimited is "max <period>" cat "$CGROUP/memory.max" # limit.memory; unlimited is "max" # Pod-level cgroup (parent slice), used by Pod-level resources cat "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/cpu.max" "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/memory.max" # Present when MemoryQoS is enabled cat "$CGROUP/memory.high" "$CGROUP/memory.min" "$CGROUP/memory.low" SCOPE=$(basename "$CGROUP") systemctl show "$SCOPE" \ -p CPUWeight -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUQuotaPeriodUSec -p MemoryMax Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path (slice:runtime:id), not a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup. Expected mapping at each layer: Kubernetes: spec.containers.resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses.resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on spec.resources and the parent pod slice. CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): cpu_shares, cpu_quota, cpu_period, memory_limit_in_bytes, plus unified for Memory QoS. crictl inspect does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them. OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period}, linux.resources.memory.limit, and linux.resources.unified. The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion. systemd scope: CPUWeight, CPUQuotaPerSecUSec, CPUQuotaPeriodUSec, MemoryMax. Unlimited or unset values often appear as  or infinity. cgroupfs: cpu.weight (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), cpu.max, and memory.max on the container scope. Memory QoS adds memory.high, memory.min, and memory.low. Further reading Kubernetes 1.31: Moving cgroup v1 Support into Maintenance Mode Kubernetes v1.36: Tiered Memory Protection with Memory QoS Kubernetes v1.36: PSI Metrics for Kubernetes Graduates to GA Kubernetes 1.25: cgroup v2 graduates to GA KubeCon NA 2022 cgroup v2: Before You Jump In by Tony Gosselin & Mike Tougeron, Adobe Systems KubeCon NA 2022 Cgroupv2 Is Coming Soon To a Cluster Near You - David Porter, Google & Mrunal Patel, RedHat KubeCon EU 2020 Kubernetes On cgroup v2 by Giuseppe Scrivano, Red Hat.
