title: [Kubernetes] Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap
summary: Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost. The node density problemThe Kubernetes ecosystem has reached a fundamental physical resource constraint: the strict limits of hardware memory versus the growing demand for dynamic, bursty workloads in the new agentic era. Historically, administrators provisioning memory-intensive workloads encountered a persistent dilemma: set memory limits too high and you waste expensive infrastructure on idle RAM; set them too low and you risk Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills. This conflict is amplified when deploying autonomous AI agents using secure execution environments like the agent-sandbox framework. These agentic pods require large memory footprints to initialize and execute untrusted code. However, after their burst of activity, they typically enter long-tail idle phases waiting for user prompts. Keeping this idle state in physical RAM caps cluster density and makes AI infrastructure expensive to run. The solution: Kubernetes node swapWith the introduction of Kubernetes' support for running nodes with swap enabled (which reached General Availability in v1.34), this paradigm shifts. By enabling the Linux kernel to page out anonymous memory to disk, node swap acts as a shock absorber during traffic spikes or periods of heavy memory oversubscription. Historically, swap was discouraged in Kubernetes for two reasons. The first was memory accounting. Under cgroup v1, the controls treated memory and swap as a single combined limit rather than letting operators set an independent limit for disk swap. Without independent tracking, a process could page large amounts of anonymous memory out to disk, which made a container's real memory usage unpredictable and hard to isolate. Kubernetes' swap support resolves this by relying on cgroup v2, whose separate swap accounting tracks disk swap on its own. The second reason was the latency penalty of paging to slow spinning disks, which fast NVMe Local SSDs largely eliminate. Together, these make it practical to increase pod density and buffer against memory spikes without sacrificing cluster stability. The benchmark dataTo quantify the performance boundaries and cost-saving potential of Local SSD-backed node swap, this analysis covers three distinct workload categories: a Traditional Build Workload for CI/CD pipelines, High-Density Browser Sandboxes, and Isolated Python Sandboxes. Workload Profile Baseline Capacity (No Swap) Local SSD Swap Capacity Density Improvement Linux CI/CD Kernel Build 600 MB RAM Limit 300 MB RAM Limit -50% RAM Footprint Headless Chrome (Kata) 40 Concurrent Pods 50 Concurrent Pods +25% Pod Density Headless Chrome (gVisor) 80 Concurrent Pods 160 Concurrent Pods +100% Pod Density Python Sandbox (gVisor) 80 Concurrent Pods 240 Concurrent Pods +200% Pod Density 1. Traditional workload: Linux kernel buildBefore exploring specialized agentic architectures, swap was validated against classic batch workloads by running a complete Linux 6.1.1 kernel build. The kernel compilation process leverages concurrent worker threads, balloons in memory to hold compiled object files, and requires a large memory spike during the brief linking phase. This workload mirrors the memory behavior of enterprise CI/CD pipelines. Because earlier compiled objects sit inactive in memory while the pipeline progresses, CI/CD jobs frequently hoard unused physical RAM, which makes them well suited to node swap compression. On a baseline node without swap, the minimum memory limit to prevent an OOM crash during compilation was 600 MB. Routing swap to a Local SSD cut the container memory limit by 50% to 300 MB without incurring any execution slowdown (in fact, it ran cleanly in 374s vs the baseline 433s). However, as an explicit tradeoff, compressing the limit further to 200 MB forced the active working set into swap, causing long I/O wait times and increasing execution time by over 40%. This reinforces that swap serves as an insurance policy for burst memory, not a replacement for active RAM. 2. High-density agent workloads: headless browser runtimesAI agent workloads frequently require manipulating headless browsers via Chromium. However, trusting external code execution often requires stricter security isolation than standard Linux namespaces. This benchmark cross-evaluated several container runtime environments. The raw logs and testing methodologies for the default runtime are available in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap directory. Unsandboxed baseline limits (runc): To test the limits of the environment without the overhead of security runtimes, plain runc containers were swept on a c4-standard-32 node (32 vCPU, 120 GB RAM). Without swap, the node exhausted physical memory and failed past 512 pods. Enabling Local SSD swap allowed the node to support 768 concurrent pods. Advanced security runtimes (for example: gVisor, Kata Containers): Enabling strict security sandboxing increases memory overhead and normally reduces pod density. However, memory swap naturally absorbs this overhead penalty. Without swap, a gVisor environment hit a hard limit at 80 pods. Local SSD swap doubled that capacity, which allowed 160 concurrent gVisor pods on a single node. Similarly, Kata Containers microVMs exhausted physical RAM at 40 concurrent pods without swap, but using GCP Local SSD swap expanded this to 50 stable Kata microVMs before CPU saturation. At these maximum densities, the per-pod latency increase is driven mainly by pods competing for CPU, not by swap I/O. An operator tuning for a specific latency target would run at a lower density than the peak numbers here and see a proportionally smaller latency cost. For a comprehensive architectural breakdown and density metrics for gVisor and Kata, see the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap Runtimes directory. 3. Beyond browsers: sandboxed Python runtimesThe advantages of node swap also extend to untrusted, isolated code-execution environments. This sweep deployed simultaneous Python sandbox sessions analyzing 5 million rows of data from the MovieLens 20M dataset, requiring a ≃375 MiB resident memory footprint per execution. The in-depth scaling results and deployment code for this sweep can be reviewed in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap Python Density directory. Without swap, heavy concurrent bursts exhausted physical memory, causing the node to hit a hard RAM limit and fail at 80 concurrent sessions. Enabling Local SSD swap offloaded dormant anonymous memory, freeing up physical RAM and preserving the node's page cache. This allowed the node to scale to 240 concurrently isolated Python sandboxes—a 3× density improvement. As with the browser workloads, the latency rise at peak density comes mainly from the sandboxes competing for CPU rather than from swap itself. Density Benchmarks with and without Node Swap How to use itIf you manage Kubernetes infrastructure for developer environments, browser testing farms, JVM applications, or AI execution runtimes, leveraging Local SSD swap can multiply your density efficiency. In Kubernetes v1.34+, node swap is Generally Available. You enable it via the kubelet configuration: kind: KubeletConfiguration apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 failSwapOn: false memorySwap: swapBehavior: LimitedSwap Pairing this upstream configuration with your cloud provider's high-speed local disk gives you dynamic memory balancing. For example, this is natively supported on Google Kubernetes Engine via Node Memory Swap configured on Local SSD profiles. To get the benefits, configure your workloads with Burstable QoS: set your container's memory limits higher than its requests. The node automatically rations fast swap space based on idle application memory usage while keeping active processes responsive. ConclusionAs the Kubernetes ecosystem transitions into the agentic era, administrators face a growing conflict between finite hardware memory limits and the bursty behavior of AI workloads. Frameworks like Agent Sandbox provide the security isolation required for running untrusted agents, but that isolation traditionally demands large amounts of idle memory overhead. By configuring the kubelet with LimitedSwap and routing it to Local SSDs, you can mitigate this conflict. Fast swap offloads the dormant states of idle agents, allowing you to increase pod density and node utilization on the same infrastructure without compromising security boundaries.

title: [CNCF] Platform engineering needs to become more human…and less
summary: Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job. If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane. Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson. Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand. And even though I was pretty consistent and logical, and so were (most of) my engineering colleagues, things could get messy fast. That’s where platform engineering came in, and that’s when I met Dan. Dan Wilson was this brilliant platform engineer at SAP/Concur. He was one of the early open source contributors to a lot of fundamental projects. He knew Kubernetes like an old friend, and he could make your cloud infrastructure sing. I loved working with Dan because he got my logically organized code to production more logically and a heckuva lot faster. A merge to main kicked off a containerized build, then unit tests, integration tests, and a security scan, and every stage had to pass before the image was promoted to the next environment. Deployments were declarative, the desired state lived in version control, and Kubernetes made the cluster match it. It warmed my engineer’s heart to watch the CI/CD pipelines hum through their stage gates. But the whole process, the whole platform, was still made for engineers. It assumed deep technical knowledge. It required strict compliance with established protocols. It wasn’t hard. It was just logical. Just a little robotic, but that was fine because it was designed for people who were a little robotic…at least a little more robotic than the average person. I mean, what engineer would try to name a production database final_v2_USE_THIS_ONE? (Several, it turns out. But they had the decency to feel bad about it.) The platform never had to defend against this behavior, because the people using it were not completely normal humans. We designed internal platforms for engineers who read the docs (allegedly), knew what a rollback was, and had a decent sense of when not to deploy. That is so Oct 2025 But then Opus 4.5 was released and everything changed. Or more specifically, everyone changed. Everyone changed from being a normal human to being an engineer…just without the pocket protectors, inside jokes, and strict adherence to protocol. The systems that took me weekends at Disney could now be vibe-coded by the receptionist in a few hours. And they would work (they might not be secure or performant, and they might be a usability train wreck, but bear with me). Everyone was now an engineer because everyone now had agents. They had their own little fleet of Dorons doing their bidding. GitHub’s 2025 Octoverse report counted more than 36 million new developers joining in a single year, more than one every second, for a total past 180 million. What this means for platform engineering is that now the humans using the platform act more like humans than they ever have. They improvise. If the form won’t take their input, they find another way in. They share the password because sharing is polite. They ask the person at the next desk instead of reading the docs, and they copy whatever worked last time, even if last time was a different project in a different region. They name things for other humans, so production ends up running something called “Q4 launch page FINAL (Jen’s edits).” These aren’t really flaws. In most of the company, they’re called “initiative”. Or “creativity”. But you might also call it “chaos”. Of course, engineers are creative too. But what we’re about to see…what we’re already seeing…is an EXPLOSION in creativity entering the software development world. Because now creativity of all sorts, from all sorts of very non-robotic people, has been given direct access to the code. Musicians. Copywriters. Recruiters. The finance lead who has opinions about dashboards. These are people who were never going to learn a programming language, and now they don’t have to. They bring taste, empathy, and a feel for what customers want, which the old pipeline often filtered out long before anything reached production. They also bring their own idea of what “done” means and no idea how a typical internal developer platform operates. But these new humans and this explosion in creativity are here. And they’re not going away. So platform engineering has to find a way to harness all this creativity without it taking anything important offline or leaking company secrets all over the internet. Making room for the more-human builders Here’s what I think needs to happen for that to take place. The rules have to move out of people’s heads and into the platform. For as long as most of us have done this work, the guardrails lived inside the engineers…at least in large part. Nobody had to tell a senior engineer not to expose a database to the internet, not to paste an API key into a chat window, or not to name a production table test. They had learned it the hard way, usually at 2am, usually once. Those lessons got passed along in code reviews, in onboarding, in the raised eyebrow of a colleague. The platform didn’t have to enforce what its users already believed. It could be a little naive, because its users weren’t. That arrangement is finished. The copywriter shipping a landing page has never been paged at 2am, and I hope she never is. The recruiter building an interview scheduler doesn’t know a public bucket from a private one, and there’s no reason she should. The finance lead with opinions about dashboards will happily connect one to the production database, because that’s where the real numbers are. They’re doing what every smart, motivated person does with a new tool: click around until something lights up. So the platform has to know these things on their behalf. Every app has to get its own identity the moment it’s created, scoped to what it needs and nothing more. Secrets must get injected at runtime, not handed to a person, so there’s nothing to paste into Slack and nothing to save in a notes app for later. Policies have to check every change before it lands: no public endpoints without a reason, no direct line from a dashboard to the production database, no resources without an owner. Every deployment has to go out small, get watched, and roll itself back if the numbers turn bad. When the platform does have to say no, it should say it the way a good colleague would. Not “Denied by policy 0042.” More like, “This would make your customer list public on the internet. Here’s the setting that keeps it internal.” An error message is the closest thing these builders will ever get to that raised eyebrow, so write it like one. Done well, most of these new more-human builders never notice any of this. And that’s as it should be. Agents, the less-human builders But wait a minute. We’ve had an explosion in human creativity entering the platform engineering chat, but we’ve also had a super explosion in agents…who are more robotic than any of (well, most of) the engineers I’ve ever worked with. Here’s what I mean. An agent will read every line of your documentation, which already puts it ahead of most of us. It follows instructions exactly. It doesn’t get bored, doesn’t take lunch, and doesn’t get a nervous feeling in its stomach before touching production. Give one a task at 6pm and it will still be working at 6am, cheerfully, having opened more pull requests overnight than your team reviews in a month. And it’s never just one agent. It’s dozens, then hundreds, each one launched by a person who has already moved on to something else. The new humans get into trouble by improvising around the rules. Agents get into trouble by following them perfectly, including the ones that are wrong and the ones you never wrote down. Ask an engineer to “clean up unused resources,” and she knows that doesn’t mean the production database that’s quiet because it’s Sunday. An agent may not. When an agent hits a wall, it doesn’t stop to ask someone. It retries, and then tries another route, and then another, until it finds a path that’s open. That’s the agent version of a marketer finding another way in, except it happens in four seconds and across forty services. And it’s always confident. (Incidentally, In all my years working with engineers, I’ve met a few who were never unsure of anything. I didn’t put them in charge of production, either.) Agents don’t learn the 2am lessons any more than the copywriter does. Most of them start every session fresh, with no memory of past outages and (just as important) none of the emotions that come with them. So what do we do about these less-human engineers? Every agent has to be treated as its own accountable actor, with limits set for machine speed rather than human speed. That starts with identity. Every agent has to have its own identity, tied to the person who launched it, with permissions scoped to the task and an expiry that matches it. When the task ends, so does the access. Then it needs a speed limit: a cap on how many changes it can make, how many resources it can create, and how much it can spend in an hour, so a loop that would have done damage at machine speed hits a ceiling instead. Agents should do their work in preview environments that look like production but aren’t, and changes should reach production only through the same small, watched, self-reversing rollouts the humans use. Every action has to go into an audit trail that answers “which agent, launched by whom, to do what.” And there has to be a kill switch that someone can find in under a minute. Most importantly, the rules have to be written down, in a form a machine can read. The unwritten rules your platform used to depend on simply don’t exist for an agent. When it breaks one, the platform’s answer should be a clear, structured reason and the specific thing to change, so the agent fixes its request instead of hammering the same door 500 times. Here’s the good news. Once the rules are written down, agents become the most reliable builders you have. They don’t argue with the template, skip the checklist, or decide the standard doesn’t apply to them this one time. Taking a page from Kubernetes I’m optimistic about our ability to build for these new platform users, and the reason is Kubernetes. We’ve solved this problem before. Just not for people. Before orchestration, running software at scale meant a person watching servers. Someone noticed a process had died and restarted it. Someone decided which machine had room. Someone approved every change. That worked with a dozen servers and fell apart at a thousand. Kubernetes didn’t fix it by hiring faster operators. It changed the contract between the operator and the work, and four parts of that contract map almost exactly onto the new builders. You declare, it reconciles. You don’t tell Kubernetes how to keep three replicas running. You say you want three, and a control loop works continuously to make it true. That’s what the new humans need. The copywriter should be able to say “a landing page customers can reach, that can read the product catalog,” and the platform works out the identity, the network, the secrets, and the rollout. Agents get the same contract in its most literal form. A spec is exactly the kind of thing an agent is good at writing. Every request goes through admission. Nothing gets into a cluster without passing the admission controllers, where policy can reject the request or fix it. The API server doesn’t care whether the request came from a senior engineer, a CI pipeline, or a script someone found on Stack Overflow. That’s the attitude platforms need now. A change from the designer, a change from an agent, and a change from Dan all go through the same door and get checked against the same written rules. There’s no VIP entrance for people who “know what they’re doing.” (Sorry, Dan.) Limits are part of the spec. A container declares the resources it needs and the most it’s allowed to use, and a namespace can carry a quota. One runaway process can’t starve the cluster, because the ceiling was set before it started. That’s the agent speed limit from earlier, and it isn’t a new idea. It’s a resource quota for builders. Assume failure, and heal on your own. Kubernetes expects containers to crash, and it doesn’t take it personally. It checks health, restarts what dies, rolls changes out gradually, and rolls back when the new version isn’t ready. Builders deserve the same treatment: assume any change might be wrong, whoever made it, and make being wrong boring. Kubernetes let a handful of people run tens of thousands of containers without knowing what was inside them. The next job for platform engineering is letting a handful of people support thousands of builders (humans, engineers, and agents) without needing to know what’s inside their heads. More human, and less Platform engineering has to become more human and less human at the same time. Less human in how it enforces things. No rule that lives only in someone’s memory. No review that depends on someone being awake. No guardrail that relies on a raised eyebrow. All of that becomes control loops that run at 3am without complaint. More human in how it talks. It takes intent instead of instructions. It explains a “no” in plain language. It lets a recruiter build something real without first becoming me. Dan used to make my infrastructure sing. The job now is orchestrating a much bigger choir: thousands of new voices, some who have never seen sheet music, some who read it perfectly and far too fast, and a few old robots like me. Kubernetes taught us how to orchestrate containers. Now we have to do the same for the humans, the sort-of-robotic humans, and the definitely-not-humans, all on one platform.

title: [Cloudflare] Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm
summary: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat, an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm called QuePaxa.QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well.Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat.Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works.What we’re building and why it’s uniqueMeerkat is a distributed system in which replicas agree upon an ordered log of events, where each event is decided by a consensus algorithm.Consensus algorithms allow a group of machines to agree on a single shared truth, even if some of those machines crash or disconnect. Consensus algorithms provide an important guarantee: machines never decide conflicting values. This ensures Meerkat replicas’ logs never diverge.Meerkat uses its consensus-powered log to expose applications like a key-value store, where each entry in the log is a get or a put. Because the consensus algorithm guarantees replicas’ logs never diverge, they all construct the same key-value (KV) state. Comparable consensus-powered systems include Consul, etcd, and Apache ZooKeeper.Unlike similar systems, however, Meerkat was designed for global scale. A Meerkat cluster may be distributed across continents and connected by links that often exhibit high and variable latency. This is an unusual setup for consensus systems, which are usually deployed in smaller, more local networks, and have strict latency requirements.The challenges of consensus at a global scaleWhile all consensus algorithms ensure that replicas agree on the same value, many of them become disproportionately unavailable or slow when network conditions degrade (but machines do not crash). We have seen this happen firsthand: in 2020, the partial failure of a core Cloudflare network switch caused a consensus-powered system to degrade and the dashboard to operate 80x slower than usual, for six hours. Critically, the system lost no data. But it became unavailable for writes until the issue was resolved, which is unacceptable.Ideally, a consensus algorithm should be able to make progress despite latency spikes and broken connections, not just replica failures. This is particularly a problem at global scale, where faults are more likely to originate in the network, and not our own servers.Let’s examine two common traits of consensus algorithms that can lead to degradation under hostile network conditions: destructive interference and fault detection. Later, we’ll see how QuePaxa sidesteps both of these issues.Destructive interference and leadersConsider Paxos, the veritable grandfather of most consensus algorithms. A lot of consensus algorithms inherit the structure of Paxos – both the good and the not-so-good bits.Leaving an egregious amount of detail out, here’s how Paxos works. There are two kinds of processes: proposers and acceptors. Abstractly, the goal of the system is for a majority of acceptors to agree on a value proposed by some proposer. There are two phases: the Prepare phase, and the Accept phase. In the Prepare phase, any proposer can send a ballot number out to a majority of acceptors. This ballot number serves as a promise – acceptors will only accept proposals with that ballot number or higher. Then, in the Accept phase, the proposer sends its proposal along with the ballot number to a majority of acceptors again. If a majority of acceptors still hold the ballot number of the proposal, the majority accepts it, and the proposer can safely decide the proposal.Challenges arise when two or more proposers submit proposals at the same time. Specifically, another proposer can interleave its own higher ballot number in between the two phases, blocking any lower ballots. Two proposers can repeatedly block each other from progressing – effectively competing for acceptance.When proposers compete and block each other in this way, we say that they destructively interfere. Destructive interference gets worse as more proposers propose their own ballots. The more concurrent proposers there are, the more likely it is that the system gets stuck repeatedly proposing. Even if none of the replicas have crashed or are unavailable, multiple proposers and misbehaving networks can block Paxos. Formally, we say that Paxos does not guarantee liveness (i.e., that proposals are eventually decided) without assuming that, at some point, all messages arrive within a bounded amount of time — an assumption known as partial synchrony.To avoid multiple proposers constantly competing, most deployed consensus algorithms, like Raft, Multi-Paxos, and Viewstamped Replication, add a special leader proposer. The leader is the only replica that can make proposals. Centralizing the proposing power in one replica forces an order on concurrent requests, avoids competing proposals, and has the added benefit of getting decisions done in an optimal single network round-trip, instead of two. While the leader is healthy and the network is well-behaved, leader-based protocols are fast.The trade-off is that the leader must remain operational and reachable. When it fails, becomes too slow, or is disconnected from the cluster, the system stalls. The only solution is for the remaining replicas to detect that the leader has failed, and elect a new one in its place.When leader recovery is unstableWhen a leader fails, the system must recover by electing a new one. Interestingly, leader recovery is often how destructive interference sneaks right back into a leader-based system.Consider Raft. For safety reasons, Raft elects a new leader using a majority vote. A replica that suspects that the leader has failed announces itself as a candidate for leadership and requests a vote from other replicas. If more than half of the replicas agree to vote for the candidate, it becomes the new leader. If they don’t, then a new election is called, and the candidates try again.Multiple replicas can become candidates — all they need to do is detect that the leader is down. The candidates may then all try to acquire a majority vote simultaneously. The problem is that the candidates will compete for the majority vote, which means Raft’s elections suffer from the destructive interference we just saw in Paxos: two replicas can mutually prevent each other from getting support from a majority and becoming the leader. The more elections fail, the more replicas will try to get themselves elected leader.Even if the leader stops being faulty, elections continue to disrupt what could have been normal system functioning. This is known as a metastable failure: a failure pattern that perpetuates itself even when the initial cause of failure is removed. A two-second network outage — or a momentarily faulty network switch — can make the leader appear to be faulty and force a leader election, which can fail, and force further elections. The outage will be over in two seconds, but the election can continue for much longer as candidates continue to block each other.Ideally, consensus algorithms wouldn’t need any recovery process, as they are complicated, prone to interference, and introduce another source of downtime.When fault detection goes awryThe problem of destructive interference in leader elections is compounded by trigger-happy fault-detection, especially in wide-area networks. In order for leader-based consensus algorithms to choose a new leader, replicas must first detect that the leader has failed. However, if replicas detect leader-failures inaccurately, the system may spend an inordinate amount of time in recovery, not handling requests.In a distributed system, where machines are separated over a network, fault detection will ultimately depend on expectations. A process cannot directly observe that a remote process has failed; it can only observe that an expected message has or hasn’t arrived. We need a predictable pattern of communication, such as heartbeats or acknowledgements, to tell us that a machine is healthy. If an expected message does not arrive within the expected time, we suspect a fault. The difficulty lies in managing those expectations.In real networks, especially wide-area networks, messages don’t always arrive when predicted. There is no guaranteed upper bound on the time that it takes for messages to arrive. That’s not to say that the network is slow, or that it is unreliable — most messages arrive within the time we expect them to. Instead, sudden bursts of latency and losses in connectivity can, momentarily, and without warning, increase the time it takes for any message to traverse the network. We call such networks asynchronous.The big issue with asynchronous networks is that if some server doesn’t reply in a given amount of time, we don’t really know if the server has failed or if the network is just slow — the two are indistinguishable over the network. Any practical fault detector has to make a guess based on how long it has been waiting compared to its expectation, and sometimes that guess will be wrong.In leader-based algorithms, that guess is exactly what triggers leader elections. Sometimes the leader is down; sometimes its messages are late, or the connection is silently broken. The protocol cannot know which one happened before it reacts. If the guess is wrong, and a replica thinks the leader is faulty when it actually isn’t, then an election begins and the entire system must stop. Until the leader is replaced, no progress is made — and as we just saw, that can take a while.Fault detection is fundamentally error-prone in asynchronous networks, and when the detector makes a mistake, we get downtime.When fault detection is slowEven when a fault detector guesses correctly, there are issues. Fault detectors react to failures by observing messages on the network, and so their response time has to scale with network latency — the detector’s timeout can’t be below the network latency. This is why Raft is commonly deployed with an election timeout of five to ten times the network round-trip time. It has to be high enough to give a chance for the leader to signal that it is alive, and avoid falsely triggering elections. The election timeout can be much lower than that, but since leader elections completely stop the system, timeouts are usually set conservatively high.Roughly speaking, a round trip halfway across the world is measured in hundreds of milliseconds. If an election timeout is several round trips, detecting a failed coordinator can take around a second. Even when fault detection is completely accurate, it is slow, and it is slowest in high-latency global networks. Until the detector reacts, the system is down.Why QuePaxa is the right fitWe realized that any algorithm relying on a strict leader or accurate timeouts was inevitably going to stall in a consensus system that runs over the Internet. We searched for consensus algorithms designed for asynchronous environments — protocols that didn't rely on a well-behaved network or precise timing to function. This led us to QuePaxa, published in 2023 by Tennage & Băsescu et al.The most notable thing about QuePaxa is how it can efficiently reach consensus in a single round trip under favorable network conditions, but also gracefully degrades performance during latency spikes, connectivity issues, and server failures. QuePaxa achieves this by solving the exact problems we just discussed through three key design choices: having an optional leader, completely removing the reliance on fault detection, and designing for constructive interference between proposers.In QuePaxa, much like in Paxos, there are two roles: proposers and recorders. Proposers submit proposals to be decided on, and recorders serve as intermediaries between proposers, recording every proposal they see.Instead of having proposers compete to get their own proposals decided, in QuePaxa, proposers will cooperatively work towards a proposal that everyone supports. QuePaxa does this by assigning a priority to proposals, in the form of a random number. The optional leader gets an exclusive maximum priority. During execution, proposers submit their proposals to the recorders, who propagate the proposal to other active proposers. When proposers receive a proposal from a recorder with a higher priority than theirs, they adopt the new proposal as their own, i.e., begin broadcasting the higher priority proposal instead. In general, proposers in QuePaxa work together to decide on the highest priority proposal that they collectively know. This means proposers can’t lock each other out of deciding on a proposal, indefinitely.The caveat is that it might not be possible to spread proposals around well enough to agree on a proposal, and so proposers have to try again, with each attempt constituting a round. However, as more proposers submit proposals, the more likely they are to converge on the highest priority proposal. This is what makes QuePaxa a randomized algorithm: the randomly generated priorities of non-leader proposers are likely — but not guaranteed — to lead to consensus on the highest known priority, in a round. Yet, given enough rounds, it is guaranteed that proposers agree on a proposal.One proposer is designated the leader. The leader is the only proposer capable of deciding in a single round trip. The leader always proposes with the highest priority; if the leader knows it spread its proposal before any other proposer, then it can decide immediately. Clients aren’t forced to make requests to the leader — any proposer can propose. If the leader goes down, then clients can keep making requests to other proposers. The leader is completely optional. The leader is simply more likely to decide, than any other proposer, and do so faster, in a single round trip.However, because the leader is the only one that can decide in a single round trip, we want to use it whenever possible. To exploit this fast path without creating a single point of failure, clients sending proposals to the system hedge their bets: they send their requests for proposals to every replica, and the non-leader replicas will wait for a small timeout, so the leader can propose and decide on its own. In our own implementation of QuePaxa, we actually deviate from the paper and have clients wait the hedge timeout instead of the replicas, to reduce the amount of messages we send over the network, but the overall result is the same.This hedging timeout is very different from the timeouts used in Raft or Multi-Paxos. It is not fault detection, and so isn’t constrained by network latency; it is locally determined by replicas and can be as small as they want it to be. In Raft, having a five-millisecond timeout in a network with 100-millisecond latency would completely freeze the system. But in QuePaxa, a five-millisecond hedge timeout only increases the number of active proposers.However, hedging isn’t free: the more proposers there are, the more proposals get broadcast, and the more likely it is that replicas fail to decide in a round. Instead, hedging provides a tradeoff: we can react faster to leader changes by lowering the hedge timeout, but we incur extra bandwidth costs and may take more time to decide. That’s a tradeoff we're more than willing to make.If the QuePaxa leader goes down, we can recover as fast as we want — we’re not bound by network latency. This is how QuePaxa gets around fault detection: since anyone can propose, not just the leader, QuePaxa can proactively deal with leader failures by hedging, rather than reacting to failures.How QuePaxa works under the hoodTo understand how QuePaxa gives us all of these nice properties, let’s look at how QuePaxa actually works. QuePaxa works in rounds made up of four phases. If a proposal hasn’t been decided on in the last phase, a new round is started, and QuePaxa starts over. At the start of each phase, proposers broadcast their currently adopted proposal to all recorders. Once a proposer receives a reply from a majority of recorders, they advance to the next phase. Here’s the general outline of the phases:Phase 0 (Propose and Adopt): Proposers randomly select a priority, send their proposals to recorders, and adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority of recorders. If it’s the first round and the leader knows its proposal reached a majority of recorders first, the leader decides immediately.Phase 1 (Spread): Proposers spread their adopted proposal to a majority of recorders.Phase 2 (Check and Decide): Proposers ask a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal seen in the previous phase. If it matches their own adopted proposal, they decide on it.Phase 3 (Carry Forward): Any proposer that failed to decide prepares for the next round by adopting the best proposal they see from a majority of recorders.Let’s walk through a couple of example executions and unpack how each phase contributes to the overall behavior we want out of QuePaxa. Each execution will have two proposers (one of which is the leader) and three recorders.The Leader Fast Path (Phase 0): The first phase does three important things: it randomizes priorities (which it must do to circumvent the FLP impossibility theorem), checks if the leader reached a majority of support first, and helps proposers converge if the leader didn't. The leader’s proposal is not randomized, and will always have the highest possible priority.In the example above, the leader's proposal reaches a majority of recorders before anyone else, and receives replies confirming it. The leader can safely decide right away. This might seem dangerous, but it is entirely safe thanks to a property called majority intersection: any two majorities of recorders always share at least one recorder. Because the leader reached a majority, any other proposer querying a majority will inevitably encounter the leader's proposal and adopt it. Since the leader’s proposal has the highest priority, any other proposer will adopt the leader’s proposal. It is impossible to decide on any other proposal.Concurrent Slow Path (Phases 0-3): When there are concurrent proposers, however, it is not guaranteed that the leader will immediately decide. The leader might fail to reach a majority of recorders first, or it might receive a single reply supporting another proposer. Let's look at what happens when another proposer contests the leader.Phase 0: Pictured below, a second proposer (shown in red) reaches the second and third recorders first. The fast path is blocked. Instead of competing, proposers adopt the highest-priority proposal they receive from a majority and move to the second phase. The two proposers could both converge to the leader’s proposal in this phase. For illustrative purposes, our example will prevent convergence by delaying the leader’s messages. Phase 1: Proposers spread the proposal they just adopted in Phase 0 to a majority of recorders. The recorders keep track of the highest-priority proposal they observe. It is a simple but critical step: it prevents the protocol from later deciding on a lower-priority proposal. This is once again thanks to majority intersection: any majority queried in the following phase must include at least one recorder that saw the adopted proposal, in this phase. For illustrative purposes, we prevent convergence in this phase by delaying the leader’s message to the third recorder, so the recorder does not adopt the leader’s proposal.Phase 2: Now, a decision can happen. Each proposer determines if a higher-priority proposal gained enough support to overtake its own by asking a majority of recorders for the highest-priority proposal observed during Phase 1. If the highest proposal returned is still their adopted proposal, they decide. In our diagram, the leader sees its own proposal returned by a majority and safely decides. The other proposer receives conflicting summaries, so it cannot decide yet. Like in Phase 1, recorders keep track of the highest priority proposal they received.Phase 3: If a proposer doesn’t decide in Phase 2, it moves to the final cleanup phase to prepare for the next round. Proposers spread their proposals again and adopt the best they find among a majority of recorders. Here, the remaining proposer discovers the decided proposal and adopts it, heading into the next round.This is deliberate — if there was some decision in the previous phase, then a majority of the recorders will have that proposal, and any remaining proposers are guaranteed to adopt it. We see here another instance of cooperation between proposers — even when a round fails, proposers try to converge on the same proposal heading into the next round.Moving to the next round: After the fourth phase, proposers move on to the next round. At this point, there is no more leader fast path, and the only way to decide is by converging in the third phase. Importantly, due to proposal adoption, it becomes exponentially easier to decide as rounds progress. The QuePaxa paper predicts that each round has a 50% chance of deciding, but in practice, that probability is much higher, thanks to convergence.Putting all four phases together, we can see where QuePaxa gets its resilience. The first phase gives the leader its one-round-trip fast path. If that fast path fails, random priorities and proposal adoption help proposers converge instead of compete. The second and third phases make it safe to decide, thanks to majority intersection, while the fourth carries what proposers learned into the next round, in case proposers don’t decide.No proposer has to detect that the leader has failed before making progress, and a failed round doesn’t throw away the work already done. When the network behaves, QuePaxa is fast. When it doesn’t, QuePaxa keeps moving.How QuePaxa makes Meerkat possibleIn our own evaluations of Meerkat, where we had servers spanning nearly all continents, we’ve directly experienced the impact that QuePaxa has on the overall performance and availability of the system. Meerkat continuously processes requests, even when the leader crashes, disconnects, or just becomes slow. At no point have we ever seen it completely stall. This is exactly what we wanted.The rate at which Meerkat handles requests has also been generally predictable. Most decisions — upwards of 95% — are made by the leader in the first phase, which keeps our throughput fairly stable. In the instances where a decision isn't reached in the first phase, the throughput drops momentarily, down to at most a third of the usual rate, signaling that three round trips — so three phases — were needed to decide instead of just one. The system slows down, but does not grind to a halt.QuePaxa also allows us to confidently switch out which replica acts as leader while the cluster is running. Since the leader isn’t the exclusive driver behind decisions and proposers are cooperative, a temporarily non-optimal leader isn’t as limiting as in other algorithms, where a leader misconfiguration could stall the system completely. We can dynamically tune which proposer is the leader without worrying too much about impacting the stability of a Meerkat cluster.What we’ll be showing nextDesigning Meerkat for a global network forced us to re-evaluate how we approach distributed consensus. Instead of sticking to familiar defaults that didn't quite fit our constraints, we looked to the decades of research produced by academia and industry. That search led us to QuePaxa.Choosing QuePaxa meant choosing a less-traveled path. It has not been battle-tested as extensively as Raft or Paxos, and we’re also extending the original crash-stop design to support crash recovery. This demands careful engineering and stronger evidence of correctness than usual systems.That is why we are formally verifying our QuePaxa implementation and Meerkat as a whole, alongside extensive simulation and fault-injection testing. Future posts in this series will explain how we verify Meerkat and QuePaxa’s Rust implementation, how we test failures that are difficult to reproduce in production, benchmarks, and what we have learned while turning an academic protocol into a production system.Stay on the lookout for further Meerkat updates on the Cloudflare Blog, and if you want to learn more about research at Cloudflare, have a look at our work at Cloudflare Research.

title: [Cloudflare] Launching the Vite Ecosystem Fund
summary: Cloudflare is distributing the first $301,300 of the Vite Ecosystem Fund to 44 projects and maintainers across the Vite ecosystem.When VoidZero joined Cloudflare, we committed $1 million to strengthen the open source ecosystem around Vite. This round is just the start.Sponsoring open source has always mattered, but now AI has made funding urgent.AI is changing open sourceAI has made open source more valuable while triggering more maintainer burnout. Previously, contributing to a project through either an issue or pull request meant you cared about it. In return, maintainers would review and provide feedback. AI changed the social contract of open source. Anyone can now create and submit AI-authored pull requests.The most visible result is the influx of pull requests. As the number of PRs has gone up, the number of maintainers reviewing them has stayed constant. So each maintainer’s workload has grown.During reviews, maintainers often find themselves speaking with an agent and not a person like they used to. If that’s the case, then why not cut out the middleman? Maintainers now have their own agents they can prompt to produce better results since they have more knowledge of the codebase.AI has raised the pressure to produce. It’s made it easier for maintainers to ship features, performance improvements, and bug fixes that would not have been done otherwise. But it’s also made it easy for other projects to do the same. When another project adds overlapping features using AI, maintainers feel a need to keep up using AI. It can become a grinding cycle, where each project pushes the other to move faster. Along the way, some projects have grown in scope and lost sight of their original goals.Maintainer burnout and sustainability have always been a problem — and now AI has accelerated those issues. That’s why sponsoring open source projects and supporting maintainers is so important in this moment.One of the Vite Ecosystem Fund’s first recipients is e18e, a community focused on improving performance across the JavaScript ecosystem. Its lead, James Garbutt, has a long history in open source, and his work at e18e has helped make popular tools like Svelte, Storybook, and Nx faster. "Sponsorships make a huge difference and allow maintainers to dedicate more of their time to the things we all rely on," Garbutt says.Fund distributionThe recipients of the Vite Ecosystem Fund were selected by a panel of core team members from Vite stack projects (Vite, Vitest, Rolldown, Oxc, Vite+), including maintainers not employed by Cloudflare.The funding is allocated through Cloudflare's Open Collective as a combination of:Contributions to ecosystem recipientsStipends to core maintainersWe’re proud that Cloudflare has committed to making the open source ecosystem we rely on stronger and more sustainable. title: [Cloudflare] The post-quantum future of web privacy
summary: The highest priorities for the transition to post-quantum cryptography are the basic building blocks of authenticated key-agreement protocols such as TLS. Without these building blocks in place, secure communication on the Internet will not be possible once cryptographically relevant quantum computers come online. However, today we rely on quantum-vulnerable cryptography for much more than TLS.Privacy Pass is a protocol used by site operators like Cloudflare to help protect applications from abuse. One way we do this is by rate limiting individual clients so that no one client consumes too many of the site's resources. Normally this involves some combination of friction or loss of privacy for users: CAPTCHAs or other challenges to moderate traffic, along with accounts and fingerprinting to identify traffic.Privacy Pass was designed to avoid this tradeoff between friction and privacy. The basic idea is that a client gets issued a number of tokens, which they can redeem in exchange for access to the site. Crucially, each token is unlinkable to the client it was issued to, ensuring the client can use the site as they always had without sacrificing privacy.With 10 years of deployment experience under our belts — using Privacy Pass for applications such as privacy proxies (like iCloud Private Relay) and relays (like Privacy Gateway) — we, along with others, are collaborating to bring the next generation of this technology to the web. One of our goals is to develop more sophisticated tools for managing agentic traffic that would otherwise consume too many resources and degrade performance for human visitors. Another goal is to foster a more open ecosystem by making it easier for more types of clients to participate. Achieving these goals requires developing new capabilities beyond what Privacy Pass offers today.Given the trajectory, in this post we look at the prospects for post-quantum. In fact, we're in better shape than one might think. Privacy Pass still relies on classical cryptography, like RSA and elliptic curves. This means that a quantum attacker will be able to forge tokens at will and use them to bypass whatever security mechanism the site operator wants to implement (such as rate limiting). On the other hand, Privacy Pass is unconditionally private, meaning no attacker, quantum or not, can link the redemption of a token to its issuance. What's more, the new capabilities we're developing for this new generation of private authentication technology can and will be instantiated in a way that upholds the same guarantee: your interaction remains private even after Q-day.This gives us a little breathing room, but we will need an alternative soon. This is an active area of research that has made significant strides in recent years. Still, just as is the case with other aspects of the transition, the primary challenge is the sheer size of post-quantum alternatives: ML-DSA-44 signatures are a whopping 2,420 bytes, while ECDSA-P256 signatures are just 64 bytes. And there's not much hope for drop-in replacements any time soon. Just as for TLS, we'll have to settle for primitives with higher cost and re-engineer our systems to bear this cost.But what will those primitives be? In this post, we'll explore one potential future for post-quantum privacy on the web, made possible by a recent breakthrough in the design of blind signatures.What we need to build: a brief look at MOLELet's start with an overview of this new technology, which is presently called MOLE ("Moderation Of unLinkable Endorsements"). We'll have much more to say about MOLE later on, but for now we'll highlight the details that are most relevant to cryptography.One of the core components of Privacy Pass is a blind signature scheme, which allows a client to obtain a signature under an issuer's secret key without revealing to the issuer the message that it signed. The client can then reveal the message and blind signature later on without linking the signature to its issuance.One type of Privacy Pass token consists of the message and blindly issued signature. To verify the token, the verifier needs the issuer's public key, and so necessarily learns the identity of the issuer. Thus while these tokens protect the identity of the client, they don't protect the identity of the issuer.Of course, this is exactly what we want for some use cases. The identity of the issuer tells us something about what type of client is connecting to our edge, a signal we use to make decisions in some of our products and for some of our customers. For instance, a client might use a token issued by one of our customers to prove it is authorized to use the customer's VPN product.However, for many use cases, this is more information than we actually need to make a decision to grant a client access to a resource. Normally we only care that the token was issued by some entity we trust. In fact, MOLE takes this a step further: the token should hide the identity of the issuer altogether so that we can't treat tokens differently based on who issued them. This guarantees equal treatment regardless of the type of client, making it easier for more clients to participate.This issuer-hiding property is achieved through a new object called an endorsement. An endorsement is issued by an anchor and redeemed by a moderator. Before redemption, the client and moderator agree on an anchor set, the public keys of the anchors trusted by the moderator. During redemption, the client proves it was issued an endorsement by one of the anchors in the anchor set without revealing which one. Upon acceptance, the moderator issues the client the MOLE credential it will use to moderate the client's interaction with the site.An endorsement can take many forms, but its key property is that it can be redeemed while hiding the identity of the anchor that issued it. There will also be many types of credentials, but because they're intended to be used by a particular moderator, they needn't be anchor-hiding or even publicly verifiable. This means that everything from blind signatures to anonymous credit tokens or anonymous rate-limited credentials can be used to instantiate MOLE credentials.Now that we have a sense of what we're building, let's look at our options for post quantum.A feast of cryptographyWhen designing cryptographic protocols, adaptability and efficiency are often in tension. Sometimes we know exactly what we want to build and can tailor a construction for that purpose; but the more we tailor the protocol for that use case, the harder it becomes to adapt that construction to a different use case.Adaptability is essential for a system like MOLE. We're not just building one kind of credential system, but many. And the types of credentials we need are likely to change over time, especially on the web where we must constantly adapt to new traffic patterns and attacker behavior. To keep up, we need a set of building blocks that can be composed together into different protocols to meet different requirements.Most of the post-quantum cryptographic schemes in wide use today come from larger families of constructions, but have been tuned for their particular application. ML-DSA is a good example here: the cryptographic framework from which this scheme was derived can be used to build a variety of things, but to make ML-DSA as compact as possible, its parameters have been carefully tailored to build an efficient and secure digital signature scheme. However, the same parameters would not necessarily be secure for other use cases.We have come to view this as the central challenge for post-quantum anonymous credentials: to decouple parameter selection from protocol design. Classical credential systems take this for granted: for the most part, protocol designers don't need to think about the parameters of the elliptic curve they're using, allowing even non-experts in the design of elliptic curve cryptography to build useful things with it. Unfortunately, designing efficient post-quantum credentials still requires an enormous amount of expertise.This situation seems to have changed, however. Earlier this year, we saw a breakthrough that represents a potential sea change for anonymous credentials.VOLE-in-the-HeadThe roots of this breakthrough go back several years. We'll pick up the story three years ago, with the VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) zero-knowledge proof system (Baum et al., Crypto 2023). A zero-knowledge proof system allows one to prove knowledge of a hidden witness, satisfying some public statement while keeping the witness private. For example, a zero-knowledge proof can be used to prove knowledge of an AES key K for which Y=AES(K,X), where X,Y are public. This proof can be transformed into a digital signature whose security reduces to the security of AES, with X,Y as the public key and K as the secret key. This is exactly the FAEST digital signature, a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature competition.Compared to many contemporary proof systems, VOLEitH is relatively simple to understand and implement securely. VOLE stands for "Vector Oblivious Linear Evaluation" and is an interactive technique that gives two parties correlated random values. These correlations act like authentication tags, allowing the verifier to check that a computation on the hidden witness was performed correctly. In VOLEitH, the prover prepares locally what the two parties would normally generate together — hence “in the head” — then commits to those values and uses the Fiat-Shamir transformation (a widely used tool in cryptography) to select the parts the verifier checks. This step turns the interactive VOLE process into a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof.Apart from its simplicity, VOLEitH is a fairly unremarkable proof system. It's not succinct in the way many other proof systems are: its proofs are asymptotically linear in the size of the witness and the arithmetic complexity of the statement being proved. However, VOLEitH is concretely very efficient for a particular type of statement, namely one that can be expressed as a set of equations over small binary fields.One example is the relation Y=AES(K,X) we just discussed. We don't normally think of AES as a set of equations, but many of its computations are designed around arithmetic in GF(28), a field whose elements are single bytes. FAEST proofs for this statement are only about 4KB (NIST Round 3, 128s).Another example is the KuMQuat signature scheme, in which the signer proves an instance of the Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem. Here we're given a system of random, quadratic equations of multiple variables over a small field, like GF(28). Mathematically, this MQ map P looks something like P(s) = (sTA1s + b1s,…,sTAms + bms) where s and each bi are length n vectors and each Ai is an n-by-n matrix. Given P,P(s) for random s, the MQ problem is to find s. We call it quadratic because we multiply the elements of s by itself.The MQ problem is believed to be hard to solve even for a quantum computer. But because P is made up of quadratic equations, proving knowledge of a solution with VOLEitH is fairly cheap, yielding KuMQuat signatures as small as 2.6KB.When compared to other post-quantum signatures like ML-DSA or FN-DSA, these numbers don't look especially impressive. But how VOLEitH compares to other schemes in a particular category of constructions is beside the point. For MOLE, we'll need to strike a balance between performance and the ability to build many types of credential systems. To that end, we need one more ingredient.Multivariate signaturesAnother way to build signatures from MQ maps involves embedding some additional mathematical structure into the map. In the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) signature scheme, the public key is an MQ map P, and a signature is a vector s satisfying P(s) = t, where t is obtained by hashing and salting the message to be signed.The secret key for this signature scheme is a trapdoor for P with which the signer can derive solutions to the MQ equations. The trapdoor reveals to the signer a hidden partitioning of the variables of each quadratic equation into “oil” and “vinegar” variables. Oil variables are never multiplied by one another, so fixing the vinegar values turns the equations into a linear system that the signer can solve for the oil values. In the public key, oil and vinegar variables are mixed together in a way that hides this structure in the map.UOV is also a candidate in NIST's ongoing signature standardization effort. It has one of the smallest signatures among the candidates, at just 135 bytes. The trade-off is that it has the largest public keys, at 46.6KB. MAYO is another multivariate candidate with much smaller public keys, at the cost of slightly larger signatures.The key thing to take away here is that the arithmetic complexity of evaluating a UOV (or MAYO) signature is comparable to evaluating an MQ instance. Both are public quadratic maps over small binary fields, making them a good fit for VOLEitH. This brings us to the breakthrough.Blind signatures from VOLE-in-the-Head and UOVEarlier this year, a blind signature called PoMFRIT was published (Baum et al., USENIX Security 2026) that achieved what at the time was a record for candidate post-quantum constructions: 6.7KB for the blind signature itself and just a few hundred bytes for issuance. PoMFRIT is based on VOLE-in-the-Head and the MAYO multivariate signature. We can easily drive the size of the signature down to 4.3KB by swapping MAYO out for UOV. (This figure uses NIST round 3 parameters for UOV (uov-Ip) and FAEST-EM-128s.) The trade-off is larger public keys, but this pays off in applications where a public key can be cached and used sufficiently often.This is competitive with state-of-the-art lattice-based constructions. But the really good news is that building blocks of PoMFRIT can easily be reconfigured into all of the credential systems we've considered for MOLE, including endorsements. More on this in a bit: for now, let's look at how PoMFRIT works in more detail.A well-known paradigm for designing blind signatures is the following. First, the client places the message in the cryptographic equivalent of a sealed envelope, called a commitment. For our purposes, a commitment is simply the hash of the message together with some randomness generated by the client. To complete issuance, the signer simply signs the commitment directly.To construct the blind signature, the client produces a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge of the signature and the randomness it used to compute the commitment, called the opening. A verifier would use the signer's public key to verify this proof.Let's define a bit of notation to make this clearer:The client generates an opening r and sends a commitment c=H(m,r) to its message m to the issuer.The issuer produces a signature s=Sign(sk,c) and sends it to the client. It doesn’t learn the message as it’s hidden behind the hash.Finally, the client produces a proof π of knowledge of s,r for which Verify(pk,H(m,r))=1,The proof π is the blind signature. It can be verified by any party in possession of the issuer's public key pk and the message m.Unlinkability comes from the client presenting entirely different objects during the two phases: a commitment is shown to the issuer during issuance, and a zero-knowledge proof is shown to a verifier during presentation. Even if the issuer and verifier collude or are the same entity, they cannot link the sessions.The size of the proof π is dominated by evaluation of the hash, so we need to choose a hash function that is friendly for our proof system. For most proof systems, such proof-friendly hashes are not well studied, but for VOLEitH it turns out that the Keccak permutation used in SHAKE and TurboSHAKE is a good choice. Keccak’s bitwise operations translate natively into VOLEitH constraints: XOR becomes addition, AND becomes multiplication, and rotations simply rearrange values. (Many popular SNARKs, by contrast, are designed for large prime fields, making byte- and bit-oriented operations less natural to express.)Nevertheless, Keccak evaluations end up being the largest component of the VOLEitH proof, so we need to make sure we're using only the minimum necessary number of permutations. PoMFRIT requires two: one for the commitment and another for the signature. Concretely, the statement we prove is roughly P(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) where s is the signature, rs is a salt chosen by the issuer, P is the issuer's UOV public key, and H denotes the Keccak permutation with the output truncated to the appropriate length, which also prevents anyone from inverting.From blind signatures to endorsements and beyondRecall that for MOLE endorsements, we need something like a blind signature, but one that doesn't reveal the anchor that issued it. That is, we now have a sequence of anchor keys P1,…,PN, and the statement we now want to prove is Pi(s)=H(H(m,r),rs) for some anchor key Pi whose index i is now part of the hidden witness.With some care, we can write this as a set of constraints with roughly the same cost: two hashes and one MQ evaluation. We need to prove a bit more about the witness. What exactly? We won't spoil it for you: ZK circuit design is part of the craft of cryptographic engineering that makes it so fun. We'll just say the kind of thinking needed here is transferable to just about any modern proof system you might encounter.Even more advanced credential systems can be constructed in this framework, including the aforementioned anonymous credit tokens and anonymous rate-limited credentials. In both of these cases, the primary cost is an additional hash or two. Each of these also requires proving that part of the witness (e.g., the credit count) is in some expected range, but this is low cost in VOLEitH.Indeed, for every construction we have considered so far for MOLE, the primary cost is the size of the Keccak evaluation and how many times we need to evaluate it. This means that finding ways to reduce the amount of hashing yields improvements across the board.OptimizationsBefore we go any further, we need to acknowledge that cryptanalysis of multivariate cryptography is still relatively immature. We have seen advances against several parameter regimes in just the last couple of years, Both UOV and MAYO have weathered these attacks well, and an outright break of UOV and even MAYO seems more unlikely with every passing year. But we should at least expect the parameters to change in a way that adds a bit of cost to our constructions.On the other hand, it's not uncommon for credential systems used in practice to adopt a less-than-conservative security posture for the sake of performance in so far as it affects forgery resistance. This typically means relying on stronger-than-usual computational assumptions. That is, it's possible that a (pre-quantum) attack might come along that breaks anonymous credit tokens, but not ECDSA, despite the fact that they both use the same elliptic curve.Using fewer hashesPoMFRIT achieved its size record by doing precisely the same thing. Recall that the blind signature requires proving two hash evaluations, one by the client and the other by the issuer. PoMFRIT observes that VOLEitH proof generation can be split into two stages. In the first stage, the client commits to a random mask. It then hashes the message normally (outside of the ZK circuit), combines the result with the mask, and sends the masked target to the issuer. The issuer uses the UOV trapdoor to find a preimage of this target. In the second stage, the client completes the proof that the preimage and previously committed mask are consistent. The hash remains part of the protocol, but the issuer — acting as the VOLEitH verifier — can compute it directly rather than requiring the zero-knowledge proof to reproduce it.This strategy substantially reduces proof size, but it also changes our security posture. The plain UOV assumption is that no (quantum) attacker can find a pre-image for a random target without knowledge of the trapdoor. The corresponding one-more-UOV assumption (analogous to the one-more-MAYO assumption in the PoMFRIT paper) neatly captures the additional information available to the attacker as a result of this kind of optimization. The assumption, then, is that this additional information doesn't lead to an attack.This assumption may turn out to be overly optimistic. Recently, researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and INRIA managed to forge a 1024-bit RSA signature using a Privacy Pass issuer as a signing oracle. Fortunately, Privacy Pass uses 2048-bit RSA, which, in concert with other defense mechanisms, provides a pretty good security margin. Likewise, for UOV we might consider using NIST Level 3 parameters instead of Level 1.In any case, a bit more study will be required before we rely too heavily on these kinds of optimizations. It's worth emphasizing that a break here would only impact an attacker's ability to forge tokens, not the attacker's ability to violate a client's privacy.Making each hash cheaperStandard SHAKE uses a 1600-bit Keccak state with 24 applications of an underlying round function. However, since the SHA-3 standard was published, many have come to believe that 24 rounds is just too much crypto. TurboSHAKE works the same way, except the permutation uses 12 rounds instead of 24. This substantially reduces the size of VOLEitH proofs. In fact, we're quite comfortable with this security margin, and not just for this application.Another change to Keccak that reduces the proof size is to reduce the size of the state. 256 bits of the state are reserved for the capacity to get 128 bits security. That leaves 1344 bits that can be hashed in one go, which is more than we need. Reducing the state by half to 800 bits leaves us with a rate of 544 bits, which is plenty. On top of that, it even increases the security at the same number of rounds, as an attacker has less to play with. The smaller state means we’re using half the multiplications in our circuit, which reduces the size of the proof.Leaning into multivariateIn an ideal world, we could avoid proving conventional hashes altogether by replacing each hash with something that composes more natively with the algebraic structure of our primitives. Indeed, those familiar with Pedersen commitments and their use in elliptic curve cryptography may wonder if commitments can be constructed from multivariate cryptography.This might look something like this: Fix public, random MQ maps F and G and commit to a message m using c=(m+F(r),G(r)). The advantage of this approach is that the degree of the constraints is the same as the degree of the constraints for the UOV signature. Not only does this make the proof smaller, it makes it far simpler, since we avoid evaluating symmetric crypto in ZK altogether.We experimented with this approach for our application, and it yielded some impressive results. However, it's not at all clear yet if the parameter regime in which multivariate commitments yield an improvement is also secure. Notably, the risk here is not just to unforgeability, but also to client privacy. A lot more study is needed.Another direction is to build an MQ-friendly pseudorandom generator (PRG).For typical VOLEitH parameters, adding an extra witness bit adds ten bits to the proof. There is a neat trick to make this a lot cheaper: only one bit of proof per bit of witness! Instead of using VOLEitH directly, we commit to a (relatively) short key. That key we stretch into a larger bitstream using a PRG with low-degree so that it can be computed cheaply in the circuit. Now, to add a witness bit w, we get one extra bit k from the PRG, and store the bit w XOR k in the proof.There is a performance trade-off: we need to compute the PRG and the witnesses start at degree 2 instead of 1. That especially increases prover time. Also the benefits on proof size only start to pay off when you need a decent number of witness bits.And of course you need a PRG! You can create a PRG using a random MQ instance, but that’s very slow and seems overly conservative. At the other end is the Goldreich PRG, which can be seen as an as-sparse-as-possible MQ PRG. We’d want something in between, but such PRGs haven’t received much study.Is MOLE ready for post-quantum?We already have post-quantum privacy today, so we have some time before we need to have a solution in place, but now is the time to develop alternatives.Multivariate cryptography looks to be a promising basis for easily building a variety of anonymous tokens and credentials. We're currently developing two schemes in this framework: VOLE-IHAT, a candidate for MOLE endorsements, and VOLE-ACT, a candidate for MOLE credentials. Our current cost estimates for these are shown in the table below. The numbers here are subject to change as we analyze and develop these constructions. We use UOV (uov-Ip) in each case, which means the public keys are all 46.6KB. VOLEitH uses the same parameters as FAEST-EM-128s:issuancepresentationPoMFRIT (with UOV)<1KB4.3KB (redemption)VOLE-IHAT5.6KB6.5KB (redemption)VOLE-ACT5.4KB12.0KB (spend)These numbers are significantly larger than their classical counterparts. This comes as no great surprise, as "PQ is big" is really the main hallmark of the transition across the board. However, replacing RSA blind signatures with PoMFRIT has comparable overhead to replacing ECDSA with ML-DSA. The runtimes of these protocols are also excellent: each operation takes just a few milliseconds with our implementation. (Runtime can be improved by quite a bit, though at the cost of higher communication.)If these numbers hold, then we've already reached an important milestone: the transition to PQ anonymous credentials for the web can now shift from cryptography design to protocol engineering. In other words, we think we can make these numbers work. For example, whereas classical blind signatures might be cheap enough to redeem on every request, we'll have to figure out how to amortize a single redemption over multiple requests.We have some work to do before we get there. First, we need to make sure our protocols are sound, in particular by producing security proofs for them that show they are secure as long as UOV is secure. Second, we need to wait a bit for cryptanalysis of UOV to catch up. We encourage cryptographers to spend time with multivariate cryptography. Once the parameters stabilize, we believe these schemes will find a place in a ton of useful applications. We've only just scratched the surface so far.

title: [Cloudflare] Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)
summary: AI Agents now act on the web for millions of people. To a Site, an Agent can take many forms. It may be indistinguishable from a human user carrying out a task, or it might look like one visitor carrying many Users. This removes the ability for the Site to recognize, serve, and hold accountable the user or users behind the Agent, and causes the Site to face the costs when something goes wrong. This post argues that in order for Sites to maximize the access they provide to Agents, the ecosystem must develop new mechanisms to preserve the relationship between Sites and Users. Traditionally, in Security and Fraud Prevention, that requires three things: Identity, Reputation, and Accountability, allowing Sites to answer: Is the person acting being truthful about who they are? Is that person trustworthy? And who answers for the action?“Personal AI Agents” (“Agents” for short) are automations that take instructions from a human (“User”) and pursue a goal by controlling a cloud computer or browser.
