title: [Pulumi] Running Pulumi Neo in a Docker Sandbox: workshop recap
summary: The more an agent can do on its own, the more infrastructure work you can hand it, as long as its limits hold when it gets something wrong. In April, they didn’t hold for PocketOS. A coding agent on a routine staging task deleted the company’s production volume in 9 seconds. According to founder Jer Crane’s account, it used an API token it found in an unrelated file. Its explanation afterward: “I guessed that deleting a staging volume via the API would be scoped to staging only. I didn’t verify.” Railway recovered the data two days later. The agent had been told not to. “System prompts are advisory, not enforcing,” Crane wrote afterward. If the prompt can’t stop an agent, the limits have to sit where the agent can’t negotiate with them. That was the premise of Neo in a Docker Sandbox, the workshop Adam Gordon Bell and I ran with Mike Coleman from Docker. So we gave Pulumi Neo two layers. The first is a Docker Sandbox. Neo runs in its own microVM and reaches only the files and hosts we allow. The Pulumi token gets injected by a proxy on the way out, so Neo never holds the real credential. The second is Pulumi itself, which decides what Neo may change and when it has to ask. With both in place, you can let Neo work without approving every step. For why YOLO mode belongs in a sandbox at all, see my August post. Mike Coleman is a Principal Solutions Architect at Docker. His running joke is that agents “want to be helpful”. It happens in his own demos: Mike Coleman I talk to people about agents a lot. They just really want to please you. I don’t know how many times I’ve done a demo  governance for MCP servers, and I’ll be like, “Can you write to my Notion page?” And there will be a policy applied to the sandbox that says it can’t. But I have a connector enabled in Claude somewhere. And it’s like, “Well, not with that MCP server, but I can use this thing over here to do it.” Mike’s answer is to close those doors before the agent finds them: Mike Coleman The more you can create an environment where these alternate avenues are roadblocked, the safer you’re gonna be with agentic workflows. That’s where we’re coming at with the sandboxes: how do we take something that is as powerful as an agent, allow it to run as close to its full potential as possible, but avoid a bunch of catastrophic things. A deleted database scores the same as a failed task Adam’s explanation of why a capable agent does this starts with how it’s trained. Agents got good at code fast. METR measures the length of software task, in human hours, that a model can finish on its own half the time, and it has doubled every few months. Source: METR, Time Horizon 1.1. Behind that improvement is reinforcement learning on coding tasks. The model gets a task, tries it many times in a throwaway sandbox, and each attempt is scored pass or fail. Every attempt runs in a sandbox that resets afterward. In that sandbox, nothing it does can go worse than failing the task. There is no downside bigger than a zero, so the model never learns that some actions are worse than others. Adam Gordon Bell In the training environment, if you solve a task, you get one point. If you don’t solve the task, you get zero. But there’s no in-between. If you destroy the entire repo, if you delete prod, that’s the same thing. You got the task or you failed the task. There’s no asymmetric downside. Production is different. Adam Gordon Bell  existing benchmarks, no matter what you do, the worst you can get on any task is: you didn’t complete it. But in the real world, some tasks have a catastrophic downside. Published coding-agent training runs such as DeepSWE and SWE-Universe use that 1-or-0 reward. Adam’s answer is a matrix with reversibility on one axis and blast radius on the other. Training happens in the top row. Production work lives in the bottom right. Adam’s rule is that agents can act on their own when there are no side effects, when someone reviews the change, or when there’s an easy way to recover. The PocketOS agent was working in staging, which felt safe. The token it found let it leave staging without anyone noticing. Infrastructure as code moves production work toward those conditions. An agent’s change becomes a diff you can preview, check against policy, and review before it reaches the cloud. Six questions before an agent gets your cloud account Before an agent gets a cloud account, six questions: Engin Diri Who is this agent acting as? What is it allowed to change? And when does it stop and ask? That last one has a history. The human-in-the-loop pattern was very, very big at the start, and everybody was like, “Hey, there should always be a human approving stuff.” Then it shifted when everything came around to the Ralph loop, loop engineering and so on. Asking was considered something which slows you down. Still, maybe very important. Where does the agent actually run? Which credentials does it hold? And what stops it when it goes wrong? Keep these questions as a loose guardrail. Six questions before an agent gets a cloud account. Pulumi answers who, what, when, and what stops it. The sandbox answers where, and it splits the credentials question with Pulumi ESC (Environments, Secrets, and Configuration). Pulumi controls that live outside the prompt pulumi neo runs Neo in your terminal (Essentials, Pro, and Enterprise editions). Its controls live in Pulumi: Neo runs as you. It uses your pulumi login and role-based access control (RBAC) permissions, and its file and shell tool calls run locally, inside the sandbox. Approval mode sets when it asks. --approval-mode manual, the default, asks before every tool call, balanced only before pulumi up, and auto never. Read-only blocks Pulumi Cloud writes only. With --permission-mode read-only, Neo can’t trigger writes such as pulumi up, but it can still open ESC environments and reach the cloud accounts behind them. To keep it out of an environment, don’t grant your user or role environment:open on it. protect: true guards against accidental deletes. A deployment that would delete a protected resource fails. protect: false, pulumi state unprotect, or --ignore-protect still gets past it. Pulumi Policies blocks unsafe changes. Mandatory policies in a preventative policy group (Pro and Enterprise editions) run on every pulumi preview and pulumi up, Neo’s included, and stop a violating change before anything reaches the cloud. The workshop’s pack included s3-no-public-acl. Pulumi ESC replaces stored cloud keys. It mints short-lived AWS credentials through OpenID Connect (OIDC) for each run. They still reach the CLI, so they limit a leak’s damage rather than prevent it. What a Docker Sandbox isolates Each agent gets its own microVM, kernel, and Docker Engine. Only the workspace is mounted (plus a read-only skills store for supported agents), but SSH agent forwarding is on by default. All outbound TCP goes through a host proxy that injects proxy-managed credentials such as the Pulumi token. The sbx CLI and local sandboxes are free; centralized sandbox, network, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) controls are part of Docker’s paid AI Governance. What changed in Docker Sandboxes since August Secrets are global and reach running sandboxes. Since v0.38.0 (August 6), sbx secret set pulumi covers every sandbox whose kit asks for it. Since v0.45.0 (September 21), changing a global secret updates running sandboxes without a restart. Sandbox environment files (experimental). An sbxenv.yaml captures a sandbox’s agent, kits, workspace, ports, and credentials for sbx env run. Mike compared it to a dev container definition. Docker now says to keep the file under version control but outside the mounted workspace, because it can run host commands. Cloud sandboxes (experimental). sbx --cloud run claude runs the sandbox in Docker’s cloud, so it keeps going after you close the laptop. It needs sbx 0.45.0 or later and a pay-as-you-go Docker Agentic Platform subscription. New signups get a one-time $250 compute credit, instead of $25, through October 31, 2026. Running Neo inside a Docker Sandbox Every script is in the workshop repo. Store the token on the host, allow ghcr.io/dirien/ in kit.allowedSources, then start the sandbox from my kit plus a mixin for the demo’s AWS region: sbx secret set pulumi sbx run --name neo-demo --kit ./01-sandbox/region-kit \ ghcr.io/dirien/infrastructure-sandbox-kit:v0.10.0 ./02-app Neo isn’t a built-in sbx agent, so the sandbox opens a shell, where pulumi whoami -v works through the injected token while the variable holds a placeholder: echo "$PULUMI_ACCESS_TOKEN" proxy-managed From the host, the workshop’s boundaries.sh checks a host the kit doesn’t allow and one it does: sbx policy check network --sandbox neo-demo ifconfig.me sbx policy check network --sandbox neo-demo api.pulumi.com Under Balanced or Locked Down the first is denied, and sbx policy log neo-demo shows what the proxy refused. The Open preset allows all traffic. Without organization governance, a request that matches no rule is blocked and queued for your approval (sbx policy approval ls). The allow-list is an excerpt. Then start Neo: pulumi neo Inside the sandbox, I think auto approval mode is defensible for throwaway work. But allowed hosts, AWS included, still receive whatever Neo sends, and ESC’s short-lived credentials reach the CLI, so keep the Pulumi controls on. The last step, Neo trying to tear the stack down and protect: true refusing, didn’t make it into the live session. Where to start In an informal poll at the end of the workshop, 8 of the 11 people who voted said they don’t use a sandbox for their agents. If that’s you, start closed: pick Locked Down when the first start asks for a network preset. Read the denials in the terminal dashboard (sbx with no subcommand) or with sbx policy log, then approve them or add rules with sbx policy allow network <host>. title: [Netflix] Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
summary: By Shreya S Ramanujam, Yongce Li, Afshine Amidi, Sina Ghiassian, Benjamin Klein.IntroductionPicture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen:If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode.A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything.“In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.”Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual. At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not.Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize:High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants.Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis.Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail (“Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?”) rises from 0.77 to 0.86, and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~69%). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses.So, what exactly does factuality mean?Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1:Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.”It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show.Let’s take another example:Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.”Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual.But what about this?Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.”Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing exposés. So then, is this a factual synopsis?Not quite! While technically true, it paints a misleading picture of the show. A new viewer might reasonably expect it to revolve around Lady Whistledown, rather than Daphne navigating the marriage market. This, too, is a type of non-factuality we want to catch.Lastly, here’s the trickiest of all:Synopsis D: “When Daphne Bridgerton makes her society debut, she catches the eye of the aloof Duke of Hastings, and the two begin a passionate love affair that sets the whole ton abuzz.”Again, every statement is true, but the phrasing is misleading. A new viewer might assume they fall in love immediately, missing the fact that their relationship begins as a fake, mutually beneficial arrangement. This is another type of nuanced error our system should flag.So now that we have an idea of the kinds of errors we care about, the real question is: how do we build a system that is able to catch both glaring as well as subtle factuality violations?Current Service and Its LimitationsOur current factuality pipeline is a straightforward, holistic LLM call. We feed a reasoning model everything we know about a title (text assets, metadata, and a detailed factuality rubric) and ask it to judge the factuality of a synopsis. We repeat the call several times to reduce output randomness, and if any run flags the synopsis as non-factual, it fails. This approach has two main limitations:High cost: Each judgment requires multiple (five, to be exact) calls to a large reasoning model over extremely long contexts (100k+ tokens), which does not scale well.Misaligned reasoning: The model can fail synopses for nitpicky reasons (e.g., “This is a show about wonderful magic” gets failed because the characters never literally call the magic “wonderful”) while overlooking nuanced errors by convincing itself they “don’t really make the synopsis false.” This misalignment makes verdicts less reliable and rationales less useful for downstream correction.Optimizing the Holistic PipelineTo understand exactly where we should optimize the current holistic pipeline, we study the current pipeline both qualitatively and quantitatively on a custom factuality benchmark that we built. This benchmark comprises synopses hand-labeled by human annotators as factual or non-factual, along with their rationales. This analysis reveals several key insights:Insight 1: Do we really need five holistic calls?Let’s think back to why we added multiple holistic calls in the first place: to reduce sampling noise. In practice, though, we see an interesting dichotomy:Blatantly true / false synopses (Bridgerton A, B): All runs agree on the verdict with near-identical reasoning.Nuanced errors (Bridgerton C, D): The model is much more likely to disagree with itself — some runs catch the error, some don’t. This is exactly where additional sampling helps.This suggests a simple optimization: A and B don’t really need all 5 calls. If we can somehow identify these “easy” synopses upfront, we can cut down on the number of calls for them, while still giving harder cases like C and D the extra calls they need.The easiest way to do this is to ask the model to output its confidence alongside its verdict and rationale. We can then separate “easy” (high confidence) synopses from “hard” (low confidence) ones and only send the hard cases through additional checks. Think of it like airport security: most bags go straight through, but those that trigger the alarm (low confidence) get extra screening.Implementing this easy fix makes our pipeline go from the current holistic model to a new “confidence gated” holistic model:Insight 2: Five identical judges calls give us no new informationWith confidence gating, our pipeline only escalates harder synopses to the full five holistic calls. But extra calls only help with sampling noise, not systematic reasoning errors: if every run follows the same flawed rationale, they’ll all reach the same wrong verdict, rendering the extra calls useless. How can we ensure that each call counts?Idea: Diversify the judges and make them specializedInstead of running five holistic judges with the same generic factuality prompt, we introduce two specialized judges that individually target the two aspects of factuality we care about:Literal Judge: Is the synopsis literally true?Implicature Judge: Does this synopsis give a false picture to a new reader who has not watched this show?Explicitly searching for specific types of errors helps us better flag both literal and subtler implicature errors. In practice, we observe that this works better than repeatedly querying a single holistic judge, hoping that sampling stochasticity will surface nuanced errors.Insight 3: The rationale reveals mistakes the verdict hidAt this point, we have a pretty good pipeline, but we’re still underusing one of the richest signals available to us: the model’s rationale behind its verdict. For nuanced errors, we often see the model identify a point of contention, then brush it aside based on a faulty assumption or because it deems the issue too minor to affect the verdict. Can we use these shaky spots in the rationale to catch (and correct) errors the verdict misses?Idea: Secondary atomic-claim checking via a router:Since our literal and implicature judges are already strong reasoning models, we ask them to additionally critically analyse their own reasoning and surface shaky spots — any doubts, concessions, or assumptions that might need rechecking. These include cases where the model:Makes an assumption.Raises a doubt that the available evidence can’t resolve (e.g., an external critic quote).Notices a contradiction but dismisses it as insufficient to change the verdict.We pass all concessions from both judges to a router model, which:Reframes them as self-contained, verifiable atomic claims, each with a materiality field specifying the evidence needed to support or refute it.Routes each claim to the appropriate secondary Stage-2 judge: a web judge for external facts (e.g., citations, media quotes, or prior work), or a source-material recheck focused on the reframed atomic claim. By pinpointing the exact point of contention, the recheck is more targeted, making it easier to mark the claim as true or false.Putting It All Together: Proposed Cascade Factuality ServiceOur findings lead to three key improvements: specialized judges, confidence-gated escalation, and targeted rechecking of shaky reasoning using a secondary stage when escalated.We implement these improvements as a tiered system shown in the figure below: every synopsis first passes through both the literal and the implicature judges. High-confidence verdicts are retained, while low-confidence cases escalate to the router and Stage-2 judges for further checking. Stage 2 can overturn the initial verdict in two cases:FAIL → PASS: All concessions, including the original failure reasons, are supported by the secondary check.PASS → FAIL: At least one concession is contradicted.ResultsBased on our discussions from above, we evaluate three different pipelines:Evaluation: Datasets and MetricsWe evaluate these systems on two datasets: show-level and episode-level synopses. Each datapoint includes a synopsis, a human gold label (factual / not factual), and the annotator’s rationale. For episode-level synopses, we additionally require that the synopsis be specific to that particular episode, not just a generic synopsis of the overall show.We focus on two main axes: Quality and Cost. The quality metrics are listed below:Recall-FAIL is our primary metric: higher recall means fewer Gold FAILs are missed. We also track Precision-PASS, which measures how reliably PASS verdicts identify Gold PASSes, and alignment with human rationales.On the cost side, we want to reduce both the average number of LLM calls per synopsis and the end-to-end cost of producing a final verdict. Latency is not our primary optimization target, but we do want to ensure the median (P50) latency does not blow up to impractical judgement times.Evaluation ResultsThe best numbers per metric per dataset are shown in bold.Note: We compared the cascade against two holistic ablations — increased reasoning effort and a smaller, cheaper model — to test if simple ablations could achieve better performance. For episode-level synopses, we also added a full-show summary to the prompt to provide context from previous episodes; we observe summaries substantially improve performance when compared to non-summary context variants, so we report only summary-based variants.Our takeaways from this experiment are:Cascade improves quality. Our primary metric, Recall-FAIL improves on both show and episode level synopses, with a limited impact on Recall-PASS. In other words, we now catch more Gold FAIL synopses without sacrificing the reliability of our PASS verdicts.Cascade is cheaper. Cascade cuts total cost by 52.4% on the show-level dataset. Cascade (with summary) is also 15% cheaper than the current (no summary) holistic pipeline on episodic dataset.Cascade’s P50 latency increases with respect to the holistic baseline. Even so, this remains within what we consider a reasonable range for factuality judgment.Simple tweaks aren’t enough. Increasing reasoning effort makes the factuality checker too lenient, while using a smaller model makes it too strict — neither addresses the underlying problems of the holistic baseline.Summary context matters for episodic tasks. Without a full-show summary, the model tends to over-fail because it lacks the context to determine whether a detail from the episode summary fits the broader storyline.Alignment with Human RationaleSo far, we’ve established that the cascade produces better verdicts: it catches more non-factual synopses and produces more reliable PASS decisions. But are these verdicts correct for the right reasons?To measure this, we use an LLM-as-a-Judge to compare each pipeline’s reasoning against the human rationale on Gold-FAIL (GF) synopses. The judge assigns a Reasoning Similarity Score (RSS) of 0 (dissimilar), 0.5 (partially similar), or 1 (very similar) based on rationale overlap.We observe that cascade is significantly better aligned with human rationale in all cases. This is a big gain — not only is the cascade giving us more accurate factuality verdicts, but it also identifies the same points of contention in the synopsis as a specialized human annotator.Conclusion + Future WorkOverall, our proposed cascade pipeline improves both cost and quality of the existing factuality service:On the cost side, confidence gating lets us avoid unnecessary calls, reducing the average cost of factuality evaluation.On the quality side, two diverse judges allow us to collect complementary informative verdicts, while the Stage-2 judges recheck and correct the assumptions behind uncertain decisions. This results in higher verdict accuracy and substantially better alignment between model and expert annotator reasoning.The cascade gives us a path toward a factuality system that is not just more accurate, but also more interpretable and self-correcting. Some future directions to consider would be:Adding multimodal inputs to help verify claims that text assets alone cannot confirm.Use the rationale from factuality checking to correct the faulty synopsis.Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
summary: Serdar Cellat, Yuchen Xie, Bernadette Marcu, Blaid Burgess, Cody Jarrett, Carlos Pereira, Qing Shi, Samuel Carvajal, Manuel Pamplona, Dorothy Jung, Feiko Ritsema, Benjamin Klein, Alex Woo, Eugene Lok, Anna Pulido, Rebecka Swe, Sanford Holsapple, Ranjith Kumar ShettyIntroductionClips in the Netflix mobile app.At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips, our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort.Our Video Resizing ApproachConverting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot.We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead.An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios.Shot Detection and SplittingFirst, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles.Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop.Focus Region DiscoveryOnce shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera.Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing.Temporal ReframingOnce we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic.The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path.Tooling and Workflow IntegrationWe integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The interface enables them to automatically generate multiple aspect‑ratio versions of a clip with smart reframing. A unified in‑app module provides intuitive shot‑reframing controls, allowing users to review the algorithm’s crops, and quickly make targeted adjustments where needed.For more complex shots or custom campaigns, producers can export the resizing parameters as XML and load them directly into external timeline editors such as Adobe Premiere. This allows agencies and external partners to start from the algorithm’s framing decisions instead of recreating crops manually or relying on tools like Premiere’s Auto Reframe. In our internal test, our resizing algorithm outperforms Auto Reframe on a curated evaluation set, so the XML export effectively brings those higher‑quality crops into external workflows. By bringing automated resizing and manual refinement into a single place, this pipeline significantly reduces production time and manual effort while preserving creative control.Video resizing interface with reframing controlsConclusionOur work on multi-ratio video resizing is one step in a broader effort to make content creation more scalable, without compromising creative intent. By pairing algorithm-driven reframing with editor-friendly tools, we’ve reduced the time teams spend on repetitive resizing tasks and unlocked faster experimentation across mobile feeds and marketing campaigns. As we continue to broaden these capabilities to new formats and workflows, our goal remains the same: to give creatives more time to tell great stories, and to deliver a consistently high-quality viewing experience for our members and fans.Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Netflix] Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
summary: By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform TeamQuasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decisionAt Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:Does any consumer still call this method?Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:What changed in the library’s public API?Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.From API Changes to Consumer ImpactExisting techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.Consider this simplified API change:public interface Client {- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);}For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind, r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_pathFROM requested_changes cJOIN quasar.symbol_refs r ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonicalrequested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.Bringing the Analysis Before ReleaseVersion-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:{ "change": "REMOVED", "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)", "affectedRepositories": 137, "versionDistribution": , "sampleConsumerLocations":  }, { "repository": "client-wrapper", "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java", "lines":  } ], "libraryCriticality": { "tier": 1, "basis": "highest-tier downstream application" }, "comparison": { "baseShaFound": true, "headShaFound": true }}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceedA Polyglot Foundation with SCIPThe shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.Moving Risk Assessment EarlierToday, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.What We LearnedBuilding this workflow led us to four practical lessons.Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possibleRelated TalksFrom Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Building the next generation of multimodal AI experiences with fal in Microsoft Foundry
summary: Microsoft and fal partner to expand video generation in Microsoft Foundry, helping developers bring creative ideas into enterprise applications.Video workloads do not all start with the same input or aim for the same result. A creative team might explore several interpretations of a written brief. A retailer might turn an approved product image into a short motion concept. An application developer might combine image generation and video generation into a workflow that takes an idea from description to frame to scene. Each scenario brings different requirements for visual quality, motion, creative control, turnaround time, and cost. All of this means that a multi-model solution is necessary to realize a full vision. Today, Microsoft and fal are helping developers find the right tools for their workloads. We are excited to announce that Kling, LTX, and MiniMax video models are rolling out to in public preview in Microsoft Foundry through our new partnership with fal. title: [Docker] Docker and ActiveState Extending Secure Defaults to the Packages Developers Install
summary: Trusted content is the foundation security-conscious organizations expect all builds to start from. Docker has made that possible for everyone by providing the foundation free. Docker Hardened Images (DHI) are open source under Apache 2.0, with a catalog of 4,000+ minimal images (and growing) built from source and continuously maintained by Docker. The catalog also carries customizable Helm charts and over 65,000 hardened system packages. For most services, adopting DHI is as simple as changing the FROM line. Teams building on a secure foundation now want the same assurance for the open source their applications install. That open source is a different layer of the supply chain, where thousands of upstream projects are pulled in at build time by pip, npm and Maven, and by coding agents as well. Docker is committed to one standard for trusted content across everything teams build on. A new partnership with ActiveState, the company that has been securing open source since 1997, extends that standard to the packages themselves. Together, we give teams the same assurance on both layers, from the hardened images Docker maintains to the packages developers and their agents install on them. Once configured, the integration allows developers and AI coding assistants to continue using familiar package managers and development workflows, while approved dependencies are sourced through governed repositories rather than directly from public registries. A hardened foundation removes a class of security work before code is written Most applications still start from a large, generic base image, and the cost of that choice keeps growing. A large image increases the attack surface and accumulates stale dependencies, and the CVEs it generates land on developers long after the image was chosen. By removing unnecessary packages, rebuilding components from source and continuously maintaining the image, Docker Hardened Images reduce the vulnerabilities inherited from the container foundation. Images can achieve near-zero known CVEs, which means less remediation work and less scanner noise before application code is introduced. The hardening and patching are handled once in the foundation, for every service that builds on it. Key takeaways When the TeamPCP campaign weaponized a widely trusted security scanner in March, Docker Hardened Images were not affected. DHI’s controlled build pipeline and dependency cooldown periods helped prevent compromised upstream artifacts from entering the image build process during the attack window. Without trusted content on both layers, your team inherits the risk Above the base image sit the dependencies an application brings with it. DHI secures the operating system packages and the language runtime that ship in the image. The application’s own libraries are pulled in at build time by its package managers from public registries, where trust is assumed and seldom verified. That layer needs what the image now has, a source that admits only the versions a team has approved and stands behind the fix when one of them needs it. Coding agents now pull those packages too. As Mark Lechner, CISO wrote in April, a compromised dependency pulled by an agent has the same blast radius as a compromised developer machine. This year’s supply chain incidents have followed one pattern. As Lechner documented, attackers steal developer credentials, use them to poison trusted packages, and the compromised packages steal more credentials. The axios compromise earlier this year put two backdoored versions of a library downloaded 83 million times a week into circulation for about three hours. Most of these attacks burn out within hours. A build that resolves fresh from a public registry, with no lockfile or cooldown in front of it, has nothing between it and a version published an hour ago. The slower failure is the vulnerability that surfaces in one of those libraries months later, when no one outside the team is accountable for the fix. Either way, without trusted content on both layers, the risk lands on your team. One standard for trusted content, from the image to the packages built on it Docker Hardened Images are the foundation, and Docker stands behind them. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, with full, unsuppressed CVE visibility. A security team can see what is in the image and how it was built. For teams that need remediation on a predictable clock, DHI adds a 7-day SLA on critical and high CVEs, FIPS and STIG variants, and secure customization on its paid tiers. While DHI secures the image, ActiveState hardens the open source built on it. ActiveState provides the Curated Catalog, a private, policy-governed repository of open source components that security teams curate and developers and AI coding assistants consume safely. The catalog holds only the packages a team has approved. ActiveState compiles every component from original source code in a SLSA Level 3 environment with full provenance and complete SBOMs, in place of pre-compiled binaries from a public registry. When a fix becomes available upstream, ActiveState rebuilds the component and publishes it to the catalog automatically under SLAs of 5 business days for critical CVEs and 10 for highs. With DHI and the Curated Catalog together, both layers carry provenance, SBOMs and a remediation SLA from the hardened image to the packages built on it. That gives security teams a consistent evidence trail across the software supply chain. The artifact repository teams already run, Artifactory or Nexus, points at the Curated Catalog as its upstream the way it points at PyPI today. Developers keep the same pip and npm workflow, and coding agents are served the governed version. None of this replaces the pinned digests, cooldown periods and sandboxed agents Lechner recommends. It gives those controls a governed source to point at. The agentic era demands trusted content at every layer AI coding agents are changing how quickly organizations create software. They can generate applications, select dependencies and initiate builds at a pace that traditional security review processes were never designed to support. Still, faster development should not mean blindly accepting more supply chain risk. Docker Hardened Images reduce the security burden of maintaining container foundations. ActiveState’s Curated Catalog extends governance and managed vulnerability remediation to the open source libraries those applications depend on. The result is a more consistent approach to software supply chain security, with trusted foundations, governed dependencies, verifiable build evidence and clear remediation responsibilities. The goal is not to add another security checkpoint that causes friction in your build process. It is to make the secure path the easiest path for developers, platform teams and AI coding agents alike. Security scales when the defaults are strong and the foundation is maintained by a team accountable for it. In an increasingly agent-driven development environment, the security of what gets built depends heavily on the trustworthiness of what those agents are allowed to consume. Docker now resells the ActiveState Curated Catalog alongside DHI, and ActiveState resells DHI to its customers. The hardened image and the packages built on it are both available through Docker.

title: [Docker] The Ecosystem is the Answer: Docker, the Blueprint Alliance, and the Importance of Collaboration in the Agentic Era
summary: In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use. Gartner expects that number to explode to more than 150,000 by 2028. Only 13 percent of organizations think they have the right governance for today, and AI is evolving and moving faster than any other technology paradigm in our history. Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway). But there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure. The good news is history has already shown how to get there. How technology gets adopted Historically, technology adoption has followed a reliable pattern. A capability spreads, each vendor and team builds its own approach, the inconsistency becomes expensive and ineffective, leading the industry to agree to a shared baseline. Adoption then accelerates. Take the credit card industry, for example. The big credit brands each ran their own security programs, and merchants had to satisfy every one. This was, of course, cumbersome for the vendors, but also for the customers, too. Every time a customer wanted to adopt a new technology, they had to manually build out security and adoption plans, adding significant adoption and procurement delays. Rather than continue on their own, the credit card companies came together to create PCI DSS 1.0 in December 2004 and formed the PCI Security Standards Council in 2006. Buyers now had one thing to ask for, and auditors had one thing to check. Collaboration overcame complexity, and everyone benefited. Security-minded technologists can find another example closer to home in the Center for Internet Security (CIS). In the early days of the internet, cybersecurity was a veritable wild west. Enter the CIS, which was founded in 2000 because the industry lacked prescriptive, recognized hardening standards. To this day, each CIS Benchmark is built by consensus among volunteer experts, vendors, and academics. Docker itself is no stranger to the development and furthering of shared standards. As just one example, in 2015, Docker contributed its image format and runC runtime to the Open Container Initiative. A shared baseline at the runtime layer let registries, runtimes, and clouds interoperate. Each of these examples played a different role: PCI mandated, CIS guided, and OCI standardized. Agents will need elements of all three. Where enterprise AI is on that curve Agents are in the everyone-builds-their-own phase. Each product solves a real piece of the problem, but which piece, and how the pieces fit, is rarely clear. “Agent governance” or even “AI governance” can mean almost anything. Adoption is incremental. A developer allows common commands, widens filesystem access, then connects GitHub, a cloud tool and an MCP server, each through a prompt that makes sense on its own. The logs mostly record that the developer acted. Security is often the last to know. The risks: familiar and new Much of the risk is familiar. Shadow adoption looks a lot like early SaaS and cloud. Credential sprawl and supply chain exposure are old problems. Inventory, least privilege, audit, and joiner-mover-leaver discipline still apply. Several things are new, however: Runtime reprogramming. Users — and the agents themselves — can change what an agent does in plain language, with no release cycle. Borrowed identity. An agent typically assumes the user’s identity, so anything the user can read, change, or delete, the agent can too. Autonomy. Agents act asynchronously, spawn sub-agents, and pass authority down the chain. A bad instruction can become an action before anyone steps in. Risky combinations. A tool with no known vulnerability can still complete a path from untrusted input to sensitive data to external communication. A shorter response window. Containment has to revoke credentials and sessions, not only kill a process. Existing controls still matter, but they were not built for this mix of programmability, access, and autonomy. How the Blueprint Alliance and Agent Baseline respond As with the credit industry and PCI, cybersecurity and the CIS, and containerization and OCI, collaboration offers the answer to this new era of complexity. That’s why Docker is not just focused on building tools like Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance, but in taking an ecosystem-centric approach to problem solving for our customers. Docker is already a founding participant in multiple initiatives aimed at developing valuable reference architectures for AI security workflows, including the Blueprint Alliance and Agent Baseline. Both start from the same premise: no single vendor or enforcement point can solve this. The Blueprint Alliance sets out how the pieces fit together. Okta, AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Docker, Google Cloud, Lovable, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler are founding members, with GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen as strategic advisors. The open, multi-vendor reference architecture answers four questions: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond? Members have committed to interoperability testing over MCP, OCSF, SSF and CAEP, and to publishing reference integrations. Agent Baseline sets out what each piece must do and how to verify it. It fills the gap between threat lists, which say what can go wrong, and the capabilities an enterprise needs in place. It defines six outcomes (Discover, Constrain, Authorize, Observe, Validate and Respond) and 35 open, versioned controls, each with a permanent identifier you can cite in an audit finding or RFP response. Docker, Snyk and Keycard drafted it, and the current release is v1.0-draft. Controls stay where they already live, in the identity provider, the sandbox and the SIEM. Blueprint says how the pieces connect. Agent Baseline says what must be true and can be checked. Both advise starting with discovery before policy, and testing the kill switch before you need it. For partners, the roles are defined. The Alliance whitepaper assigns integrators the operating model: assessing a customer’s current stack against the architecture, assigning ownership across the pillars, tiering risk, and running lifecycle and compliance over time. Technology partners get a published target to integrate against, and the reference integrations cross vendor lines by design. The partners who can design, integrate and operate across those lines are the ones customers keep. Where Docker fits Most Alliance members govern agents from the outside: who the agent is, what it can reach, and what it is observed doing. Docker governs the inside: the environment where the agent executes. As agents move from suggesting actions to taking them, trust has to extend beyond the model to the places where they run. Docker has helped define a shared baseline for the runtime before, and now we’re working with the Alliance and our partners to make that baseline concrete, open, and testable in the age of agents. The execution environment is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced. That boundary is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced. The Alliance whitepaper notes that without runtime support to pause an agent without collateral impact, API-driven containment “provides a false sense of security.” Agent Baseline’s CON-03 calls for isolated, confined execution, which is the job of Docker Sandboxes, while Docker MCP Gateway and Docker Hardened Images cover tool access and the supply chain.The Secure Software Factory reference architecture, drafted in part by Docker authors, applies Agent Baseline to agents that ship code. What to do next Baselines let adoption move faster, not slower. Security and platform leaders can assess against the baseline today. Agent Baseline controls are citable, and Okta offers an AI Blueprint Assessment Tool. Partners can start with the Docker Navigator Partner Program, which rewards AI governance work, and with the reference integrations the Alliance publishes. Docker’s VP of Partners Leon Jones explains the program here. Download the blueprint at blueprintalliance.ai and read the controls at agentbaseline.org.

title: [Docker] Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?
summary: Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work. You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work. Mounting a repository from your host Sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox: $ cd ~/my-project $ sbx run claude Open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host. This fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout. NOTE: Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment. Give each task a separate working tree Git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward. There is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status. sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout. Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout. Keep the project inside the sandbox A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout. This workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote. One sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too. Those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory. That independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser. For a web app preview, ask the agent: Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0. Then publish the port from another terminal on the host: $ sbx ports my-sandbox --publish 8080:8080 Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem. An environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there. Choose the repositories for the job An API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward. A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree. The same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices. Combine the choices to suit the work The checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself. The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.
